utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has to take the oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will -- let the witness take the oath, and let me have a copy of the summary. I don't have one. Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please state your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Petar Kriste, Dubrovnik, on the 5th of January, 1936.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a Croatian citizen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I'm an economist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the Minister of Defence of the government of Croatia for several months in 1990; and if so, during which time exactly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, I was. From the 30th of May until the 24th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given your professional background and not being a professional soldier, why were you elected into a position of Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Croatia, in those days after the first multi-party elections, was constituted as a democratic republic, and it was generally believed by the leadership of Croatia that it was normal for a civilian to head the ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thus at that time while you were the Minister of Defence, did you expect any violent developments within the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I personally feared that that could happen. However, Croatia did everything to avoid it. What is more, after the peaceful transition of power in the top leadership, the conviction spread that violence could be avoided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you replaced and by whom?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I was replaced on the 24th of August by General Spegelj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular reason for doing this at that time, replacing you as a civilian with a general?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. On the 17th of August, there were large-scale disturbances or, rather, a rebellion in the area of Knin and a part of Lika. Actually, citizens of Croato-Serbian ethnicity put up barricades, stopped vehicles, searched them, and a larger-scale rebellion was instigated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You continued to be -- did you continue to be a member of the government; and if so, in which period and what function?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I was a member of the government right up until the 15th of April, 1992, and I performed the duties of Trade Minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation regarding the TO, in particular TO weapons, when you took up the duty of Minister of Defence? Did you have any control over weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: When I took over duty, the Territorial Defence had already been disarmed. Actually, the Yugoslav army had taken the decision after the first round of the elections that the Territorial Defence in Croatia, Slovenia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina should be disarmed. And this was carried out, the formula being that the warehouses were unsafe where the weapons of the TO had been stored until then and that it should be placed in safer warehouses, that is, under the full control of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your time as Minister of Defence, did you make suggestions for changes in the TO; and if so, what kind of changes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. The Territorial Defence, according to the constitutional system that was in force, was simultaneously a component part of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, but it was also the territorial army within the jurisdiction of the republic. That territorial component of the armed forces, according to the constitutional provisions that were in force and enshrined in the constitution of Yugoslavia and of Croatia, the republic took care, prepared, organised and commanded the Territorial Defence. However, when the party that won at the multi-party elections took over power, the commander of the republic Territorial Defence Staff refused to cooperate with the new leadership, and my proposal was that he be replaced and that the Territorial Defence be adjusted to the constitutional frameworks that were in force or, rather, that it should be placed under the control of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your suggestion followed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No, it was not accepted. President Tudjman wanted at all cost to avoid any conflict, and he especially wanted to avoid a conflict with the Yugoslav People's Army. So that was the reason why he did not accept my proposal at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to get control over weapons? Did you do anything in relation to TO weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: We asked the federal minister of -- no, of national defence, that is, Mr. Veljko Kadijevic himself, and also through General Novoselic, who was commander of the republic staff of the TO in Croatia, that the weapons be returned. However, those weapons were never returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in your time as the Minister of Defence, did you purchase weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After General Spegelj replaced you, did he purchase weapons; and if so, when and what kind?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, while I was the minister, had requested from the federal authorities additional weapons to arm the police, the regular and reserve force of the police, which had been increased somewhat. However, the federal authorities rejected that request as they did the request for returning the weapons of the TO. After that, as far as I can know, but I did not take direct part in this and I don't have any precise information, but a certain quantity of light infantry weapons was procured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: This was at the end of 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Spegelj also make suggestions for preparation of a defence, an effective defence, and if so, how did President Tudjman deal with it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I know that General Spegelj drafted three plans for the defence of Croatia. However, those plans were not discussed at cabinet meetings, so I do not have detailed insight into the -- what actually happened with those plans. But judging from what Mr. Spegelj himself told me, as well as some other colleagues, President Tudjman rejected all three defence plans prepared by Spegelj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did he do that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I think the reasons were the same as when he refused my proposal for changes in the Territorial Defence. He wanted, at all cost, to avoid the war and conflicts primarily with the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After -- during the time in the government now as the Trade Minister, did you get information that in the course of 1991 Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic met and negotiated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Such information was never received officially by the government. However, in the Croatian press, there was a brief report at the end of March 1991 that Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic had met in a frontier location between Serbia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Later, it was learnt -- I think that that note itself did not mention Karadjordjevic, but subsequently, it was learnt that it had taken place in Karadjordjevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a brief conversation with Mr. Susak that related to this meeting in Karadjordjevo in March 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No. I did not have a direct conversation with Mr. Susak about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have -- did you meet Susak or did you come across Susak at that time period, and did he tell you something?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Shortly after that, ten or 15 days later, I couldn't say exactly when, I met Mr. Susak. He was in a rather good mood. And when I asked him for the reason of his good mood, he told me that a decision had been taken, or wording to that effect, that Herzegovina should be annexed to Croatia. At the emotional level, I could understand that, because Mr. Susak was a native of Herzegovina, and it was natural for me that he should be glad if that part of Croatia were to be part of the Republic of Croatia. But on the other hand, such a report disturbed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he indicate who made such a decision?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me who had taken the decision. He just said, "I'm coming from the leader and such a decision has been taken." This could not have been a formal decision. My understanding was that this was an informal discussion during which such an agreement had been arranged or reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this reference to the leader, does that mean President Tudjman? Was he referring to Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Susak, at that time, was he the Minister of Immigration?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he close to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss with colleagues what was the topic of meetings with Milosevic -- between Milosevic and Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: We were all surprised by this news report itself that Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic had met, and of course it aroused a great deal of interest, and there was a lot of talk as to what could have been the content of that discussion. Though we did not have any confirmation from official sources, we thought that it could have been a kind of bargain struck between Serbia and Croatia taking into account certain divisions within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now move on to Dubrovnik. Before and during the war, did you yourself focus on what happened in the region of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I did. During the war, I was in Dubrovnik just before the beginning and during the beginning of the war, then on three other occasions during the blockade and occupation of the region around the town, and once immediately after the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from the area of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the end of September, beginning October, were you present in Dubrovnik; and if so, which dates?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I was in Dubrovnik from the 26th of September until the 5th of October. That was the period I spent there and that was when the actual heavy attack on Dubrovnik itself started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you -- why did you go to Dubrovnik on the 26th of September? Was there a particular reason?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: There was. We had received quite reliable information that an attack on Dubrovnik was forthcoming. And also in view of the forces, and we knew exactly how strong they were and what their distribution was, what their deployment was, that they were ready for an attack to Dubrovnik, and our assessment was that our forces were absolutely weak and that they needed to be reinforced, especially with weapons, because there were enough personnel in Dubrovnik itself ready to defend the town and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Marinovic request weapons or other support from the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: General Marinovic, who was then lieutenant colonel, asked for aid in weapons, and he addressed a fax to that effect to Zagreb, and my colleagues from Dubrovnik advised me to do my best to have the request sent by General Marinovic fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the -- what did General - or Colonel then - Colonel Marinovic request, and did he get what he requested?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I did not have insight into the actual list, because in his fax he had specified exactly what was essential for the necessary defence. But I do know that I and my colleague Jurica, who also was a deputy in the Assembly and who was also a native of Dubrovnik, like me, we didn't bring even a part of what he had asked for. Actually, we didn't bring any weapons. We brought a truckload of mines and explosive devices, which were certainly useful and necessary, but General Marinovic was concerned and worried because there was a shortage of infantry weapons and especially there was no heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't he get that? Was it not available, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Croatia was not prepared for war. I already said a moment ago that Croatia wanted to avoid the war at all costs. But at one point in time, it even believed that this would be possible. For this reason, and also because every conflict wanted to be avoided with the JNA, the necessary preparations failed to be made, and especially the procurement of certain quantities of weapons or their manufacture in our own facilities. In view of this, when the attack on Dubrovnik started in Croatia, there really were not available the quantities of weapons necessary to meet General Marinovic's request, but my impression was - this may be subjective and a subjective impression - that as much as could have been done was not done probably because the organisation was lacking as the preparations for defence had not been made in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Dubrovnik, what did you find in terms of defenders? How many people were there to defend and what kind of people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: When I arrived in Dubrovnik, I found some 300 defenders on the outside, and these were the members of the regular police force. There was a small unit of the National Guards Corps, and people who until then had been civilians and who, as soon as the threat of an attack occurred, reported themselves and wanted to take part in the defence. There were quite a number of these people, but there was a shortage of weapons for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In regard of professional soldiers and policemen, how many policemen, can you say approximately, and how many soldiers, National Guard? If you could say. If you don't know, then --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about the citizens that -- how many -- did they have uniforms? Those citizens that took up arms, did they have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No. At that time throughout Croatia, very few people actually had uniforms. Those who had uniforms were policemen. They were the only ones. And some of the members of the Croatian National Guards Corps. The young men went around in sneakers and civilian clothing, and that's how they fought, all those who were able to get any weapons. And they, of course, were included into the organised defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they actually -- did they volunteer to help, to defend the town, or were they compelled to do that? I'm speaking of the young men.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. They were volunteers. They came forth quite freely. And let me repeat that far more reported for duty than we could take in because there were just enough -- not enough weapons to go around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of weapons did these people have?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Mostly they were infantry weapons; ordinary rifles and a few automatic rifles of the Kalashnikov type.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had information about the other side, of the troops of the other side. What was that information? How many Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. soldiers were on the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: General Marinovic in Dubrovnik, according to a previous agreement, had arrived from Trebinje, where he was the commander of the Trebinje garrison of the JNA, and he had exact facts and figures about the troops that were directed against Dubrovnik. And according to what he told us, in the first squadron there was about 5.000 men with 105 artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit the --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: They had the support of tank units and the air force from Mostar and from some other places. So they were in the first echelon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit the village of Brgat, together with ECMM observers, on the 27th of September; and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: On the 26th of September, when we arrived in Dubrovnik, we received information that at the borderline between Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina there were -- there had been a number incidents taking place and that the attack had in fact already begun, and particular mention was made of Konavle and the boarder with Montenegro and the access towards Trebinje. And it was for this reason that we decided to go to Konavle straight away on the 26th, when we arrived, to see what was going on there, especially Molunat because people said that an invasion was being prepared there. And we arrived there, as I say, on the 26th. First of all, we took the road to near Molunat and we really did see that there were two naval ships belonging to the Yugoslav navy, but they were not anchored there, they were cruising along the coast. When we approached Molunat itself, gunfire was opened -- they opened gunfire and attacked our vehicles and so we withdrew towards Grude. Mortar fire and grenades followed us from the surrounding hills. And it was due to these onslaughts, rather even before we arrived in Dubrovnik, the villagers of Molunat were displaced and were put up in the hotel at the Babin Kuk area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I actually didn't ask you to go into that many details, but just one side question: Did you travel in a civilian car or was it military?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: In a civilian car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my question was: Did you visit the village of Brgat together with ECMM observers and why?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, the next day. On the following day, which was the 27th of September, we did visit Brgat, yes, because we had also received information that up there at Brgat several grenades had been fired. So we went there together with the ECMM monitors to visit the village. And we did come across some -- a few houses that were partially damaged. One of them was completely damaged. And according to a soldier, he said that this -- the shell had come from the Bosnia-Herzegovina area, and Brgat -- Brgat is right near the border.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the Exhibit 337. It's -- in the atlas you cannot see the place Brgat. The witness can -- should point it out on the ELMO because on this atlas you can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We seem to be having some trouble with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have actually indicated the place Brgat with a red tab. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, that is Brgat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a connecting road to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Brgat is right on the road running from Dubrovnik to Trebinje. It is just one kilometre away from the BH border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This place Brgat, did you expect -- the defenders and you, did you expect an attack coming through this road?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, an attack was expected. And as I say, from the eastern side, from the Montenegrin area, it had already begun earlier on. And we expected it to spread along this road too, because in fact that is the only road along the Trebinje-Dubrovnik axis. So we were expecting an attack, and as I have already said, there were certain military operations under way, that is to say, several projectiles had already hit when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there also a Croatian defence in Brgat? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: At that point in time when we were there, we didn't notice anything of that kind, any other military units. We just saw the damage that had been done, and the villagers told us that the damage was done during the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's enough. We don't need the map any more. At that time, did the Croatian authorities or the Croatian population in Dubrovnik region endanger the Serbs in the region?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No. There was no threat to the Serbs in the region. And let me also say that there's a relatively small percentage of Serbs living in the region. Approximately 5 per cent. And they lived under normal conditions. There were never any incidents on that basis, ethnic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they - I mean the Croatian authorities, Croatian population, Croatian defenders - did they pose a threat to the JNA at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No, no threat whatsoever, and that for two reasons: First of all, because Croatia did not want a war. It wanted to avoid a war at all cost. And it was would be ludicrous that with the forces it had at its disposal that the Dubrovnik defence should engage in any offensive operation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Croats shoot or shell into Montenegro or Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I know quite certainly that there was no shelling of that kind. The situation was quite the reverse, as I have described it; from Montenegro into Konavle and from Bosnia-Herzegovina onto Brgat and the Dubrovacka-Zupa area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had there been any incidents at the border between Croat and Serb or Montenegrin forces? I mean on the 26th, 27th of September.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: At that time in that border region, there were very few of our own forces there to begin with, a few policemen, and they did not open fire at all, nor did they resist any kind of resistance. And at that point in time, the enemy couldn't be seen. He was across the border and was opening fire onto this area here along the border in Konavle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this shooting and shelling started, did the Croatian population flee their villages along the border?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: From the village of Vitaljina, which is right along the border with Montenegro, the population fled to Dubrovnik or, rather, they had gone to Dubrovnik before we arrived. And on the 26th, when we were in Konavle, people from the other villages had also withdrawn and gone to Grude in large groups, in Konavle, and they were getting ready to move on, to continue their journey towards Dubrovnik, and there were some ten policemen accompanying them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the local authorities try to make contact with the JNA to avoid the war at that time? We don't need many details, just a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: With representatives of the JNA, no, I don't think there was any contact, but the local authorities did contact the local authorities the other side of the border, in Trebinje and in Herceg-Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA or political authorities that you just mentioned in Serbia or Montenegro, did they make any demands to the authorities of Dubrovnik that could have avoided the war? Did they make any demands, what the people in Dubrovnik should do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no explicit demands made of any kind, and I can say that mostly they said that matters would quieten down, that everything would be settled and that an attack would not take place. At least, that's how I understood the people who entered into contacts of that kind say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the state level in Croatia? Were any demands made in relation to Dubrovnik at that time? I mean, on the state level; Croatia, Yugoslavia. Were any demands made in relation to Dubrovnik that the government of Croatia did not comply with?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: There were no such demands. Had there been, I would certainly have known about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was Dubrovnik attacked? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Dubrovnik was attacked within the complex of a general plan of attack on Croatia, which was an expression of Greater Serbian politics. And according to that plan, Yugoslavia was to be re-centralised, or the second variation, which had been completely accepted at that time, was to change the internal borders within Yugoslavia, rather, to push the borders of Serbia further towards the west so that, as they used to say on the Serb side at that time, that all the Serbs would be living in one state, in a single state. So that, by and large, would be the Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag line and in that area or, rather, to the east of that area was Dubrovnik, and so within that general operation, Dubrovnik was therefore attacked. The fact that this was part of the plan was testified by Kadijevic himself in a book, in his book, and he explicitly states the units that were to attack Dubrovnik and from which axes, to join up with the forces on the Neretva River and continue their advance towards Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kriste, beyond what is in the Kadijevic book, what are your other sources of knowledge, would you tell us, as to this attack being part of a broader plan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, as a man who was active in the sphere of politics before the democratic changes in Croatia and Slovenia, I paid attention to what was going on on the broader Yugoslav level, and these demands for a change in the constitutional order or, rather, with the overthrow of the constitution dating back to 1974, in Serbia, we had clear-cut views, and it was along this line that the leaderships were toppled in Vojvodina and Kosovo and also in Montenegro. The autonomous state of Vojvodina in Kosovo was rescinded. Everything was organised along the lines of mass meetings, mass rallies of allegedly jeopardised Serbs in Kosovo, and rallies of this kind were being organised in Ljubljana --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Forgive me interrupting. These, I take it, are matters of general knowledge and part of your experience and conclusions which you've drawn from what happened. But can you help us more particularly as to any particular source of knowledge - anything anybody said to you or any meetings you had or anything of that sort - in which you gained further knowledge that there was such a plan. Do you follow? We need to have specific evidence, if we can, on that sort of topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specific evidence of that kind I do not have. All I can say is that we discussed it at closed government meetings and that similar arguments were put forward, of the type that I have just stated. But a document testifying to that, I did not see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you say discussed it, this was amongst yourselves on the Croatian side, is that right, that you came to that --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would just like to put page 135 in the B/C/S version to the witness. It's from the book of Veljko Kadijevic entitled "My View of the Break-up --" "My view of the Break-up, an Army without a State."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Kriste, did you read that book? You referred to the book. Did you read it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it. I have it here with me, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the book? You have the book with you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please put the English version on the ELMO. On this page, there was a paragraph where General Kadijevic speaks about the creation of a new Yugoslavia made of nations -- up of nations which so desire, and he also refers to the -- how the JNA would assist and the principal ideas in relation to the JNA, and I would like to quote to you: "The task of deploying the JNA in this phase of the war in Croatia was: To protect the Serb people in Croatia in such a way that all regions with a majority Serb population would be completely freed from the presence of the Croatian army and the Croatian authorities; to pull the JNA out of Croatia by first ensuring that the above task was completed; to carry out the continued country-wide transformation of the JNA into the army of the future Yugoslavia, focusing on its internal national and organisational structure and its territorial location." And he further on that same page then writes about the principal ideas, the "total defeat of the Croatian army if the situation so allowed, and certainly to the degree that would enable fulfilment of the set goals; full coordination with the Serb insurgents in the Serbian Krajina; completion of the pull-out from Slovenia of remaining JNA forces; full awareness that the role of the Serb nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be instrumental to the future of the Serb nation at large. The location of JNA forces were to be adjusted accordingly. And actually, at the end of the page, there is the mentioning -- a mentioning. It says: "The directions of offences -- offensives of the main forces of the JNA directly connected to the liberation of Serb regions in Croatia and JNA garrisons deep inside Croatian territory. To this end cut Croatia along the following lines: Gradiska-Virovitica; Bihac-Karlovac-Zagreb; Knin-Zadar; Mostar-Split." And in relation to Dubrovnik, it continues: "At the same time, strong forces from the Herceg Novi-Trebinje region would be used to block Dubrovnik from land and break out into the Neretva valley, thus linking up operations with forces working along the Mostar-Split line." Did you see that the JNA did accordingly, or what did you see happen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, the JNA did act according to this plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. Thank you. But let's return to the Dubrovnik region. Was it attacked on the 1st October -- the 1st of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, it was. In the early morning, at around 6.00 a.m., was when the area of Dubrovnik proper was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just overlooked -- we would like to put this as the first exhibit for this witness, and we have not yet an exhibit number, and this would be tab 1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit number 370.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the JNA troops subsequently take over the region around Dubrovnik town?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The forces of the JNA went around Dubrovnik, blocked it off, encircled it, and almost reached the Neretva River. That is to say, the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina, where Bosnia-Herzegovina comes out onto the sea at a place called Neum from the Dubrovnik side. And I can't tell you about the other axes. But the town itself was heavily shelled already on the first day, that is to say the 1st of October, and in the first onslaught, the power station was destroyed, 11035, via which the Dubrovnik area received its electric power. The waterworks, the water pipelines were also destroyed, and there was an air attack on Srdj and the transmission stations there, so that Dubrovnik was left without any electricity, without any water, without any telephone communication and all other communication as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness -- Mr. Kriste, I do not want to go into all the details of the attack because we have other witnesses to come. Therefore, I would like to just ask a few specific questions in relation to what happened. In which place did actual fighting between -- in this time where you were there, in which places did actual fighting take place between Croatian defenders and the opposing army? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: In those first moments of the attack, there was no actual combat, no actual fighting, because it was from the border regions that the JNA and other forces working with it launched a heavy shelling attack on the town itself and other areas from their own territory. So there was no defence because our side did not have the necessary artillery pieces. Later on, when I left Dubrovnik, the attacks were mostly launched on the eastern flank, and our forces put up as much resistance as they could along the axes ranging from Herceg-Novi or, rather, the border with Montenegro towards Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did fighting take place in Brgat in the beginning of the war? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: As far as I know, the fighting took place there somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the JNA suffer severe losses in that time period while you were there until the 5th of October? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No, it did not. It did not suffer heavy losses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the takeover of the region around Dubrovnik, were Croatian settlements or property deliberately destroyed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. The Croatian settlements were razed to the ground. Houses were set fire. What was left standing was destroyed by grenades, shells, and the whole area was looted extensively. I was able to see that throughout the region, the region that was under the occupation of the Yugoslav army, once it had withdrawn, immediately after its withdrawal, in Konavle, in Ston, and the Dubrovnik-Primorje area. I was able to see that for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in Dubrovnik in beginning October, was the old town targeted? Just this brief period.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Not at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit Dubrovnik at the end of October together with the president of the SFRY, Mesic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to get to Dubrovnik, did you have to request permission of the JNA command in Belgrade to do so?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: We couldn't get to Dubrovnik because in -- we were blocked in the Mljet canal by the Yugoslav navy, by five or six boats, and we spent the whole day there, trying to negotiate with the command in Belgrade that it allow free passage to the convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who finally allowed your proceeding to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No explicit permission was actually granted because Mr. Mesic, who was formally at that time the commander of the Yugoslav navy, did not manage to get in touch with anyone except with, I think, Admiral Brovet. So after spending a whole day there in the Mljet canal, we left during the night quietly, and we travelled slowly, and in the morning we reached Dubrovnik. So I think there must have been some kind of a tacit permission given, because there were no armed attacks against the convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not want to go into any details of this visit which lasted only for one day, is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: One day. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, together with two other members of the Croatian government, go to Dubrovnik again at the end of November 1991 to get involved in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness tab 2 of Exhibit 370. And it is, actually, a decision made of the 30th of November 1991 to send you, Minister Cifric, and Minister Rudolf to Dubrovnik, and it gives also your tasking; that is, establishing and keeping contact with the international organisations, negotiations with the JNA command, organising the return of the temporary immigrated population, and some other tasks. Is that a document that relates to your mission?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is also a reference made to the Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staffs in certain villages, including the town of Dubrovnik. What kind of Crisis Staffs were they? Were these civilian organs, military organs? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Crisis Staffs were civilian organs, and their purpose was, in those exceptionally difficult circumstances, to organise the life of the population and to provide logistic support to the defence forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to get access to Dubrovnik, did you get permission by the JNA command to go there? I mean the headquarters in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Without such permission, we could not legally enter by naval or ground routes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave the permission? Do you know that? Who in person?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Admiral Brovet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, on your way to Dubrovnik, did you spend a day in Split and got involved in negotiations between the Split authorities and the commander of the JNA military naval district, General Nikola Mladjenevic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did. Mladenic, I think his name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these negotiations, were they related to the withdrawal of the JNA from the region, and what was it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, they were related to the withdrawal of the navy and the JNA from the Split area, from Lora harbour, of the navy in the immediate vicinity of Split, and on the return of the weapons of the Territorial Defence. So these two issues were linked together in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was an agreement reached?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your arrival in Dubrovnik, did you attend negotiations on the 5th of December in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides you and the other two ministers, Croatian ministers, who was present?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic and Captain -- Frigate Captain Sofronije Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what capacity did Admiral Jokic take part?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: In the capacity of a representative of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That is how we had prepared the agreement, and also the agreement that we signed, both in the signature and the heading, it says that the negotiations are being conducted between the Croatian government and the Supreme Command, represented by Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What function did Captain Jeremic have, and did he actually get very much involved?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he actually participate much in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: He did not participate. He was just physically present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did your delegation request? And how -- can you describe how the negotiations went.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: We requested, first of all, that there should be a serious truce. Then we requested the lifting of the blockade of Dubrovnik and the Gruz harbour. Then we also requested that the JNA allow electricity and water supply systems to be repaired so that the population - and there were about 40.000 inhabitants at the time - could receive power and water. And generally, we wanted to supply the population -- to ensure for the population of the city somewhat better conditions of life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did General Jokic respond to this? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: General Jokic said that we could discuss this as well as the possible withdrawal of the JNA to some more distant positions only on condition if Dubrovnik was freed of all our forces. And he said there were 15.000 such forces and described them as Ustashas and mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you respond to this? Can you tell us about the exchange that you had with Jokic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Of course we could not accept such a request. First of all, there were no such forces in Dubrovnik. And secondly, the withdrawal of our forces would mean allowing free passage for the JNA into Dubrovnik. That is why we said that in Dubrovnik there really weren't 15.000 armed men but that there were 5.000 well-armed men who were ready for battle, that these certainly were no Ustashas or mercenaries but mostly citizens of Dubrovnik who were prepared to defend their city and Croatia; that we would not pull out those forces because we cannot do that because in that case, the Yugoslav army would immediately enter Dubrovnik. The admiral angrily responded, asking us don't we trust the word of honour of a Yugoslav senior officer. Our answer was no, because a short while ago, we had had a similar case. At previous negotiations, which were attended by representatives of the local authorities in Mocici near Cilipi, the Dubrovnik airport, the JNA had promised that it would not move forward its lines towards Dubrovnik but that it certainly wouldn't enter Cavtat. And as soon as our negotiators had left - they hadn't even left Cavtat to reach Dubrovnik - when the Yugoslav People's Army walked into Cavtat. Jokic stopped for a moment, but then he asked another question: "Do you think that the Yugoslav People's Army doesn't have the strength in spite of the forces you have in town to capture the town and place it fully under its control?" Our answer was: "Yes. Your forces are far superior, and in the final analysis, you could achieve that. But as long as our forces are there, you wouldn't do that, for two reasons: First of all, you would have to destroy the town itself, and you won't do that because, after all, you are afraid of the reaction of international public opinion. And secondly, you would have to count on every street and every destroyed building being turned into a bunker, and you would have very heavy losses in manpower, and you can't do that on account of your own public opinion. And that is why, for as long as the defenders are in town, we can be sure that you won't enter it." After that, he made a short break and then he made various suggestions to us, various options; that our forces should be formally disarmed, that we take -- that this be recorded, that they needed that for their own public, and then that those same forces could return to Dubrovnik via a route that was still operational across the islands of Dubrovnik, and then that we should issue a joint declaration in which we would say that we would disarm and withdraw our forces, which would unpublished in Serbia and Montenegro to appease public opinion there, which of course we couldn't accept because we realised that these were tricks. Finally --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. You mention -- what you just described, his suggestion, is that more or less a sort of fake withdrawal so that the JNA wouldn't lose its face, or what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, approximately that is what it meant. The JNA, because of its own public opinion - that is what he told us - cannot make concessions to our side without achieving its main goal, and that was the withdrawal and disarming, complete disarming, of our forces and their departure from Dubrovnik. They couldn't do this because of their own public opinion, and that is why he made these propositions which we realised or understood as being a trick, actually a fake withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question: You mentioned 5.000 people that could fight the JNA in the town. Did you actually have 5.000 people or why did you say it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: We didn't have that many people. We had a far smaller figure, around 300, maybe 400, up to 500 men perhaps. But we had to mention this figure because if we were to reveal the true state of affairs, the army would have no reason to negotiate with us but would -- could simply enter the town. We were actually negotiators of the Croatian government rather than informers for the JNA, so we didn't provide accurate figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an agreement reached, finally, on that day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, an agreement was reached which we considered to be quite favourable, because the regime of the sailing of ships in and out of the Gruz harbour was improved, and also the repair of electricity and water supply systems was envisaged as well as the road to Cavtat, which had been completely closed for the past two months.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness an exhibit that is already tendered in evidence and was used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, before removing the previous exhibit, which is tab 2, I wonder if the witness is able to tell us who is Dr. Franjo Greguric who is referred to as president at the end of the document. Second page. Was he the president of the government of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. He was the president of the government of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to this document that is now in front of you, this is actually the agreement signed on the 7th of December, 1991. But if you look at the agreement, at the articles in this agreement, was that actually the state of affairs that you had reached on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, it was the agreement reached on the 5th. All these points had been agreed on the 5th of December. However, at the end Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the discussion on the 5th of December, Mr. Jokic did not wish to sign this document, claiming that he doesn't have the authority to do so from the superior command and that he needed consultations, and that is why he proposed that we meet again the next day to sign the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You can leave the document for a while with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- on the -- when you returned, when you returned to Dubrovnik, on your way to Dubrovnik, did you actually think now an agreement is reached and the war would be over in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: We were satisfied with the contents of the agreement reached. However, we were concerned that Mr. Jokic had not signed the agreement. Nonetheless, we reckoned that the following day the agreement would indeed be signed and that thereby far more favourable conditions of life would be ensured for the population of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came back to Dubrovnik, did you have a conversation with Colonel Marinovic; and what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Returning to Dubrovnik, we informed the local leadership and Commander Marinovic as to what we agreed, and we reported to him on the meeting in Cavtat. Mr. Marinovic did not share our optimism, and he informed us that, during the day, movements of the Yugoslav army had been observed at Bosanka and Zarkovica and that he feared that an attack would be launched. This certainly affected us too so that our optimism suddenly declined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, did an attack on Dubrovnik occur starting with an attack on the Croatian position on Mount Srdj very early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe what was going on from the Hotel Argentina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: From the Hotel Argentina, already around 6.00 when the attack started, we could see that the Srdj fortress overlooking the city, that firing with artillery weapons was being done and that tanks were on the move. A little later, the fire moved towards the town itself, including the hotel that we were in, but especially the fire was targeting the old city nucleus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While this was ongoing, were you in contact with Commander Marinovic, Colonel Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, we were. We had contact with Colonel Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Marinovic try to assist his men on Mount Srdj by firing from any position within the town and, if so, do you know where the position was?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic informed us that an attack by strong forces of the Yugoslav People's Army was being launched against the Srdj fortress and that the crew could not prevail without support, and he said that he would assist from positions in the still unoccupied part of the Dubrovnik area. The exact deployment of those mortar batteries that our defence had at its disposal I am not familiar with, but I do know that in the old town itself and its immediate vicinity, there were no artillery weapons nor any military installations or facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the shelling of the old town start and what did he end? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The shelling of the old town started around 7.00, and it lasted intensively up until 1.00 p.m., and then it resumed early evening but of lesser intensity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you in possession of a tape showing this shelling, actually a tape made from the Hotel Argentina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I have this tape, and the shelling of Dubrovnik was filmed by an amateur, a receptionist at the Hotel Argentina, so I was able to see him filming it. Actually, the filming was done from the same position from which we were observing what was going on in town. Of course, what can be seen on film, on tape, is not as impressive as what we saw with our own eyes, because this went on all day and projectiles of various types flew over our heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you receive the tape and what else is on the tape besides this, what the amateur filmer made?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: On this tape, in addition to the shelling of the town on the 6th of December 1991, there is footage also of the town after the shelling, filmed the next day - that is on the 7th of December, 1991 - and also a few clips from Television Belgrade and Television Montenegro's programmes. The shots of the appearance of the town after the shelling were taken by this same amateur, and the footage from Television Belgrade and Montenegro were something that he added on to his own tape, and these were broadcast on the 7th of December on Croatian television, namely, Croatian television received the signals of Belgrade television and Montenegro television and taped some of their programmes and then rebroadcast them in a programme called TV Isbor or TV Selection, and this programme was aired on the 7th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you get the tape? Who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I was given this tape as a gift by a policeman of ours who was in our escort while we were in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has actually provided this tape to us and we have it here as tab 3, and a transcript of parts that we would like to play, the transcripts belong to this tab 3. The tape as such is quite long. It's 45 minutes or even more than that. We only want to use five minutes of it. Not the damage part but about three minutes of the actual shelling observed from the Hotel Argentina and a few clips of what was said on the TV in Belgrade and on the TV in Montenegro. Altogether, it's approximately five minutes, and I wonder whether we should play it before the break or after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it's ready to be played, we'll play it now. If not, we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, we'll play it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, they made small breaks between the sequences that are on the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be your view? That would have been your view, Mr. Kriste?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what is burning there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Probably cars that were parked on the corner. And now these are boats burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that actually the boat that you were using for the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: One of the two boats was used to go to the negotiations the previous day, to Cavtat. You can hear the explosions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, you can see here the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the time actually the tape -- the time that we saw on the tape, was that the time when it was filmed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We would now have to hear the voice. You have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And you are clearing the way for those who are 20 to 30 kilometres ahead of you. Have you been doing it successfully? "Well, successfully. So far, quite successfully. You can see yourself how fast we have gone through it. We hope that we are going to be even faster. Now we have taken this territory, next week we are maybe going to take some other territory. "At the same time, we have reliable information that Ustasha formations, especially foreign mercenaries who don't care about Dubrovnik, are preparing the scenario of its destruction in order to accuse the JNA of that act of vandalism. It is being reported in a communique from the information service of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. "Because the needs of both the current and the possible future tasks require stronger concentration of forces, mainly of means of support and artillery means, in order for our soldiers, through the use of artillery, to be exposed as little as possible during the operations regarding the taking over of particular buildings and the breaking of ZNG and MUP forces on the lines used by units. "All information presented to our public regarding the JNA using artillery on Dubrovnik is not true and is pure fabrication. It is being reported in a communique of the information service of the Military-Naval Sector Boka. In its operations carried out so far, the JNA has not fired a single shell on Dubrovnik. "It has been reported that Dubrovnik suffered damages. Is that true? "Reports that Dubrovnik was shelled or damaged or hit are not true. "Are they trying to mine the old town or a part of the old town? "That is part of the scenario they have been preparing since the beginning and which is now being carried out. While they were trying to accuse the JNA of not respecting cultural monuments nor world cultural heritage which the old town of Dubrovnik represents. They were and still are preparing mines in the old town itself which they later activate, and they then give reports that the JNA is hitting the old town. "There are another two kilometres to Dubrovnik from here. That means that we are almost in Dubrovnik. "Behind the hill. From there you can see Dubrovnik. We have stopped here. We won't go further. But if they continue to open fire from their side, then we're going to go further. But they are encircled from the other side and all around Dubrovnik so that their MUP members are surrounded and they have nowhere to go. We are now just waiting for the order to advance towards them in order to disarm them."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So that's the tape. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That's a convenient moment. We will adjourn now. Mr. Kriste, in this adjournment and any others there may be, could you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, let me get back to the question I asked during the first session. I couldn't follow, frankly, the answer of the accused. Was Mr. Greguric another name for Mr. Tudjman? The witness said that Mr. Greguric was the president of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, of the government, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of the government. At the end of the tab, Greguric is the president of government. It's different from the president of Republic of Croatia. Could you explain, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Greguric was the Prime Minister. He wasn't the president of the state. And that is not another name for Mr. Tudjman, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That seems to tell all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kriste, given the limited -- the technical limitations of -- in this courtroom, in the original tape that is now also as a copy with Your Honours, could you actually see the shells hitting, coming in, flying in and hitting the buildings on the original tape?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, you could see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, you couldn't see it here in the courtroom, but if you review the tape, it's very visible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from where did the shells come in? Who was doing it? I mean, land forces, sea forces, air? Who did it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: On that particular day, the ground forces were taking part as well as the navy, but predominantly it was the ground forces from the land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we heard, in the comments from the -- from officers, there was one allegation made by one of the officers and he said on the TV that the Dubrovnik representatives would prepare mines that they would activate and then report it as shells from the JNA. Did that happen? Was that done?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That is a pure fabrication and part of the propaganda which was supposed to justify what the JNA did in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were tyres burned to give the impression that the town was burning, or was it actually burning?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: It was actually burning. And on that particular day, nine houses were completely burnt down to the ground, and about 600 projectiles of different sorts fell on the town. Tyres were not burnt, however, tens of cars were on fire, parked behind the city calls, and as the cars were on fire, of course their tyres had to be burning as well. And the cars were set on fire with the shells that fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness tab 4 of the Exhibit 370, and that's actually a map showing the old town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this kind of map -- are you familiar with this map, and can you tell us who produced the map?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this map. I have a copy of it. And it was compiled by the expert services of the municipality of Dubrovnik in cooperation with the corresponding UNESCO services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that nine buildings were totally destroyed. Are they indicated with this total black -- could you maybe point, use the pointer and show us how they are indicated on this map.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: These buildings are marked in black on this particular map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these other little triangles, what does this indicate?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: They are the hits, direct hits with different projectiles. It ranges -- there are dots and triangles. I'm not quite sure what the difference is between the dots and the triangles, but on my copy of the map, all the direct hits are marked with dots. So they were probably direct hits and the damages caused by indirect hits. I don't know. I can't really say. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, why don't ask you the interpreters to translate the legend for us. Show them first.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Could the interpreters just tell us what the dots and the triangles mean. You should -- actually, I just -- I'm just told that you have a translation, and I also overlooked it. We have a translation, actually, given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Also I overlooked it. We actually have the explanation what the legend means. So, yes. I think that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I want to ask you one more thing in relation to this map. Could you indicate on this map where the car parks -- where the car parks were that you just mentioned that cars outside were burning. Could you point out where the car parks would be.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The car parks would be on the northern side of the ramparts, of the wall, in this area here. There are several parking spaces, parking lots, and they're all interconnected, and it's this general area here and here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: On the outer side of the wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing at the top of the map where there are square -- square places behind the walls, on the other side of the walls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. In addition --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many -- how many people were killed on that day? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Nineteen civilians were killed and about 60 others were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the old town, were residential areas also targeted, in particular hotels with refugees?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were targeted. Actually, the whole of the town was targeted. It was shelled all over, both residential buildings and hotels in which the refugees had been put up. And there were about 15.000 of them altogether in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any military targets or positions in the old town on that day? Did you see any outgoing fire from the old town?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No, not from the old town. There wasn't a return of fire, any outgoing fire from the old town. And not only the old town but in the immediate vicinity of the ramparts, the walls. And we, from the hotels, were not able to see any point from which they opened fire, from which there was a return of fire. And of course, you can see the old town quite well from the hotel where we were put up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Croatian side provoke the shelling in the first place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No. The Croatian side did not provoke any shelling. Quite the reverse; the Croatian side expected a secret truce to be signed and the agreement that we had agreed upon on the previous day in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the shelling took place, did you reach Admiral Jokic on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as the shelling started, we tried to get into contact with Admiral Jokic. However, we weren't able to reach him to begin with, and then later on, with the help of a satellite telephone, we were able to set up connection with him and able to talk to him on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you speak to him for the first time and what did he say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: We spoke to him for the first time somewhere after 8.00 and he first said that there was no shelling, that he didn't know about any shelling. On the second occasion, which took place half an hour or an hour later, he said that he did know that there were clashes going on but that it was our side which was to blame because it had attacked the JNA units in the Zarkovica and Bosanka area. We relayed this on, and we, of course, said that that was not true. On the third occasion, he admitted that there had indeed been an unfortunate incident, as he put it, and he apologised for it, claiming that it wasn't his order that led up to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that third telephone call, when was it approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, it could have been sometime around 12.00 or a little after 12.00. Between 12.00 and 1.00. I can't give you an exact time, but it was after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you believe what he said, that he didn't order it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No, we didn't, of course, believe him, because an operation of that sort cannot be conducted by anybody, any subordinate, on their own bat. It could only have come from the Supreme Command, which was embodied in the person of Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when -- when he said that he didn't order it, did he promise to stop it or did you talk about how to stop it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. And we agreed, first of all, that the cease-fire would take place at 11.00. However, even after 11.00, there was still shooting until dusk, although it is true that, after 1.00 p.m. in the afternoon, it was of lesser intensity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where Admiral Jokic was when you reached him in the morning on these three occasions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: We assumed that he was somewhere in the Bay of Kotor, but I don't know the exact location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to reach him in Kotor? Is that where you tried to find him, or why do you think he was there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: We tried to reach him in Kumbor, in Herceg-Novi and all these other places, I think in Kotor, the town of Kotor as well. Now, where we actually found him, I can't say, or where he contacted us from, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to reach him another time after the shelling continued? You said on the third occasion you actually expected it to stop. Did you try to reach him another time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: We received later on, sometime around 2.00, 1400 hours, a radiogram, in fact, in which Jokic informed us about the fact that an attack had taken place contrary to their own will, and he apologises and says that General Kadijevic had ordered an investigation into the whole matter. And he also said that during -- in the course of the afternoon, he would have to travel to Belgrade so that we would not be able to have a meeting, the meeting that had been arranged in the course of the morning for that particular day. But we couldn't bring about the meeting because of the continuous bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could the Exhibit 361, tab 45, please be put to the witness. It's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is this the fax message that you were talking about? And it's actually in English language. Do we have a B/C/S? No? Okay. Maybe we put it on the ELMO. It's -- Do you recall that it was a message in English?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I think we received this fax in Croatian. I had the text of this fax in Croatian. I don't know whether the original might have been in English or not and then translated, but I had the Croatian version myself. But I do recognise it. Yes, I recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we put it on the ELMO, and could the translation -- the translation booth just read the first paragraph message, starting with, "Your Excellency," so that the witness can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Your Excellency, I express my sincere regret for the difficult and unfortunate situation that has been created. This was not our order, neither was it close to my sanity to opt -- to act like this. General Kadijevic has sent a message to you and the ECMM in Dubrovnik on undertaking energetic investigation on our responsibility and the guilty ones for this event. At the same time, we expect to find out the responsibilities on your side for the sake of a thorough clarification of all circumstances in regard with the events from last night and this morning. General Kadijevic has invited me to Belgrade at 1400 hours, so today I will not be able to continue the negotiations with you. I suggest the following..."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We can stop here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you received?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is the content.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you -- are you aware whether an investigation actually took place and whether any officers were ever charged or disciplined for any unauthorised actions in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I don't know that anybody was charged or disciplined because of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after receiving this fax, I understand from your statement the shelling continued but to a lesser extent?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That's right, yes. The shelling continued, and you can see that from the footage. It went right on until 1600 hours, when it became dark, and that's when the shelling stopped. But the buildings were still on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have already now seen the document the agreement of the 7th of December, 1991. Were the same persons present, that is you - the three ministers - and Admiral Jokic and Jeremic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That's right, yes. The same persons on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you protest against the shelling, or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: At the beginning of our talks, the representative of the observer -- European observer mission protested. And after that, we launched our protest, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Admiral Jokic's reply?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic repeated what he had said the previous day; that he was sorry that the event had taken place but that it was not pursuant to any order of his. And he also informed us that on the previous day, he had been to Belgrade where he had talks with Mr. Kadijevic and that during the night, the representatives of all the western embassies had lodged their protests with the Supreme Command because of the bombardment of Dubrovnik and that, for that reason, Mr. Kadijevic was very angry himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this agreement, then, was signed in the way as it was already agreed upon on the 5th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA film the damage done to the old down the following day? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I do know about that.
