At the end of this conversation, the talks we had with -- on the 7th of December, Mr. Jokic asked us to secure a television crew of three or four persons which would come to Dubrovnik to convince themselves of the damage that had been done and that was talked about, so that that could serve as evidence in the investigation to be conducted by General Kadijevic. And indeed, they came the next day. I didn't meet them, but I do know that the crew did come and did film the damages around town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The agreement of the 7th, was it complied with? Did the shelling then stop?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: On the 7th, there was no shelling already on the 7th, and for quite a long time there was relative calm in Dubrovnik. It was only later, in 1992, that there was shelling on several occasions once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the JNA, or then the VJ, withdraw from the region?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I think it was in June or July that the JNA withdrew, but I'd have to check that out. But they withdrew from the western part of the municipality and reached Cavtat, the vicinity of Cavtat, and they stayed there until the middle of October 1992. They finally left the entire Dubrovnik region in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the questions that the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kriste, at the beginning of your examination-in-chief, you explained how you became the Defence Minister of the Republic of Croatia after the elections in 1990, and you said that because of the development of democracy, it was decided that the Minister of Defence should be a civilian. How was that possible that the development of democracy lasted for such a brief period of time, just several months, and then General Spegelj was appointed to that post nonetheless later on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I have already said that in August 1990, there was a rebellion on the part of the Serbs in Croatia and that it was a large rebellion, and then it was assessed that it wouldn't progress as smoothly as we thought without clashes and conflict as we had expected at the beginning, right after the democratic elections had taken place. So the rebellion had -- was on such a broad scale that already at the beginning over 25 per cent of Croatian territory was outside the control of the Croatian authorities, and we expected that the rebellion would spread, of course with the support of the JNA and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the reason for that rebellion? You mentioned the events in Knin and the barricades that had been set up. So what came prior to those events? What happened before that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: What happened before that were rallies that were held in Knin in 1989, as early on as that, and then at the beginning of 1990 as well. And they followed the pattern of the same types of rallies that were held in Vojvodina and Montenegro at which slogans were being shouted out, saying, "This is Serbia," and, "Give us arms."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And tell me, if that is so, if the rallies were of this nature, for example, in that area, Lika, Banja, Kordun, in that general region and so forth, the region -- and you considered them to be nationalistic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, then, was it possible in that region with very few examples of four municipalities, the Serb population had a majority vote for Racan's party, the SK of Croatia, the League of Communists of Croatia, and it later on changed it name. You know the election results, you're aware of them. And in Western and Eastern Slavonia, the vast majority voted for that particular party and 21 Serbs became members of the Croatian Sabor or parliament?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, this was a well thought out, organised activity, directed from Serbia and which endeavoured in every possible way to turn the Croatian Serbs against the newly established authorities that were proclaimed -- they proclaimed it to be Ustasha authorities without any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reason at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was there any reason for the Serbs to be upset in view to the -- with regard to the events that took place, the log revolution that came before? Do you know anything about how the Serbs were excluded from the constitution of Croatia as a constituent peoples? I'm sure you know about this, you're aware of that; you were a minister in the government. So do you happen to know that an order was issued to disarm the police stations, the majority of which were Serbs? Because the majority population in those areas were indeed Serb so it was quite logical for the policemen in those places to be Serb policemen too. Was there good reason for them to be upset and afraid?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, there weren't any serious reasons for them to be upset. The truth is that there were changes to the constitution, in the formulations of the constitution, but the Serbs did not substantially lose anything. In fact, according to the new constitution, they were treated first and foremost as a national minority, which -- or, rather, just like all the other parts of the population living in Croatia, as is defined in the legal systems of other countries as well. And they were also guaranteed a high level of autonomy in the local community. Now, as far as disarmament is concerned, the disarmament of the police stations, what I can say on that score is the following: The police stations in those municipalities were not disarmed. The surplus weaponry was taken away from those police stations and was taken over by the Ministry of the Interior. And the police -- the Serbs in the police were not in the majority in those particular municipalities, and in the Internal Affairs Ministry too there were far more Serbs. That is to say the ratio of Serbs was greater than the ratio of Serbs in the population of Croatia. And I can also say that the same situation was reflected in the Ministry of Defence. In the Ministry of Defence itself, when I arrived, I found 48 per cent Croats there, working there, and out of the total population the Croats make up 79 per cent. At that time, they made up 79 per cent of the total number of inhabitants. There were 32 Serbs, and the other 12 per cent were declared as Yugoslavs, and nothing happened to any of these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the dismissal of Serbs from the police, from the public administration, even health institutions, en masse? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Serbs in Croatia, while Yugoslavia lasted, was over-represented, as I have just illustrated with this example from the Ministry of Defence. And the situation was similar in the Ministry of Interior. However -- so some changes were necessary. And I personally believed that the balancing of the national composition of the employed with the composition of the population should be done gradually. The ministry should have been expanded with the employment of new staff and then things would be brought into harmony. But in some cases, different measures were taken and there were some rhetorical remarks that were not acceptable. But all of this could not have been a reason for the Serb rebellion. It was just a mitigating circumstance that helped the Serbian police to win over as many Serbs as possible for the uprising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the Republic of Serbia have any influence over the structure of the police, the public administration, the Defence Ministry that you inherited from your predecessor after the change of government? Did Serbia have any influence over that situation or was that the normal order of things in the Republic of Croatia up until then?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Serbia did not have any direct influence, but the overall situation in Yugoslavia was such that the Serbs were preferred and that via facti they were over-represented everywhere; in the economy, in the health service, in the administration, and especially in the sensitive areas such as the defence and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who preferred them, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The overall climate that prevailed in Yugoslavia at the time in which Serbia dominated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you're claiming that Serbia dominated in Yugoslavia up until 1990.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that for several decades since the war there was only one president of the federal government or the federal executive council who was from Serbia, whereas throughout the rest of the period they were mostly from Croatia and also some from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Key positions in the army, the police, in financial institutions that were all concentrated in Belgrade were nevertheless held by Serbs. Now, whether there were more Prime Ministers from one or other republic, I would not be able to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these key institutions that you are referring to were located in Belgrade, I assume, because Belgrade was the capital of Yugoslavia and that's where the federal government was based, the central bank was based there, and all the other ministries were based there. And do you know that the structure of the federal government, the composition, and of the central bank and other key institutions mostly reflected the structure -- the ethnic structure of the population of Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The top leadership mostly, yes, but the key operational positions were held by people from Serbia. And even the Presidency of Yugoslavia, which consisted of eight members representing the republics and the provinces, it operated in that way only briefly. And after you took over power in Serbia, then something very strange happened. You revised the constitution, abolishing in fact the autonomy of the provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo but you retained the representatives of those provinces in the Presidency and in other federal bodies. Similarly, by overthrowing the legally elected government in Montenegro, you acquired a fourth representative. So out of the total of eight members of the Presidency, Serbia actually controlled four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Serbia take part in the changes of government in Montenegro at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: It must have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who, for instance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: It is well known how the change of government occurred in Montenegro. The so-called endangered Serbs from Kosovo travelled like a circus around Yugoslavia, organised rallies, street demonstrations, and provoked dissatisfaction; and in doing so, they were undermining the government. Obviously, they couldn't do that on their own, that this was organised by the secret services, because tens of thousands of people cannot be moved by one person, nor can they do it spontaneously. And behind all that was Serbia's policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know all that? On what ground are you claiming that? Do you have any data, any information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: You never certified a statement to that effect but that was quite obvious. You didn't do anything to stop this wave of rallies across Yugoslavia, but instead you supported it. And when such a rally was scheduled in Ljubljana and on the way back it was due to be held in Zagreb, and when the Slovenian government prohibited such a rally, the Serbian government broke off all economic relations with Slovenia and Croatia. Actually, it started a merciless economic war in which it completely destroyed the unified Yugoslav market, the monetary system, the customs system. So all this happened even before the outbreak of the war in response merely to this decision to prohibit the rally. It caused real chaos in the Yugoslav economy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you remember to what extent the Serbs were endangered in those days? Do you know that 40.000 left Kosovo under pressure and threat and murders and torchings only in the period between 1980 and 1990, and that they were protesting why no one was protecting -- protesting why no one was protecting them. And they appealed for understanding from all the other Yugoslav peoples for the suffering they were exposed to and for the pressure and terror that they were suffering. Don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I do remember how all that looked in Yugoslavia in those years. I know what I have said, that you say 40.000 were expelled. Forty thousand people cannot be spontaneously organised. And what were they to do in Novi Sad, Titograd, Ljubljana, Zagreb? Nothing else than what they did do, that is, to cause disorder which was meant to undermine the existing authorities and bring to power your supporters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you know that there were only a hundred, couple of hundred of them who went to other parts of the country to inform the people and the authorities of the terrible conditions under which they were living and to appeal for them -- to them for solidarity. There was no violence, as you know. No one was hurt. Even the newspapers reported that not a single flower was trampled upon in those demonstrations and rallies. These were rallies of solidarity with those who were suffering in Kosovo. Don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I remember that as part of Serbian propaganda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kriste. I see that you have your stereotype opinion in that respect, which is not really customary for an intellectual who I see has published two books here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, let us refrain from these sort of comments. It's not going to take us any further. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please -- we'll come to that. You quoted here from Kadijevic's book. You said that you have it. True enough, it wasn't you that quoted from it, it was the lady opposite who quoted from it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I have the book here on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the name of the book, please?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: "My View of the Break-up," if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as far as I know from those days --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: "My Understanding of the Break-up," yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those days, the JNA spoke about only two goals that it had in those days; to protect those endangered, regardless of their ethnicity; and secondly, to protect its own units that were blocked all over Croatia. So answer my question now, please, since you are talking about this axis, Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag, then the Neretva River valley that Kadijevic refers to, were these movements of forces to enable the pull-out of the units that were blocked, as you know well, in a large number of towns where they had been stationed for decades - that is the garrisons in Croatia - or was this some kind of conquest of territory in favour of some sort of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: In Kadijevic's book, there is reference to an aggressive strategic operation which clearly determines its goals; to cut Croatia along the mentioned axes, including this breakthrough from the south, this advance from the area of Trebinje and Herceg-Novi which was to have linked up with the forces on the Neretva, and to continue towards Split. I don't know who they were liberating and who they were protecting, that is, the soldiers of the JNA in the territory of Dubrovnik, Dalmatia, and in all these other areas. Do not forget, Mr. Milosevic, in that area which the JNA was liberating or protecting the Serbian population, in 1991, there were about 2.200.000 people, out of which 1.600.000 were Croats and about 400.000 Serbs. Who were they protecting?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to this area around Dubrovnik later, because there's a great deal of confusion there, Mr. Kriste. I don't know whether you're aware of that fact, but you were explaining that you didn't talk to representatives of the JNA, but you spoke to local leaders on the other side of the border in Montenegro and Herzegovina. And then the lady opposite asked you, And what was the outcome of those talks with the authorities in Montenegro and Serbia? and you then explained that these were normal discussions. You failed to hear that she mentioned whether you spoke to anyone in Serbia. Did you speak to anyone in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I didn't say that I had talked to representatives of the local authorities in the neighbourhood of Dubrovnik, in Bosnia and Montenegro. I said that such discussions were conducted by representatives of Dubrovnik municipality. And I also said that no direct requests to the effect, "You do this, otherwise we will attack Dubrovnik," that no such statements were made as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But will you answer my question: Did you ever in those conversations have occasion to talk to any representative of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any delegation of Dubrovnik talk to any representative of Serbia? Does it appear to you rather logical -- logical for anyone in Serbia or Serbia to have aspirations to take control of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to be as illogical and senseless as you would want it to appear. It is well known that Serbia always had aspirations towards Dubrovnik, that in Serbian cultural circles Dubrovnik was referred to as the Serbian Athens; and the attack on Dubrovnik was certainly part of a broader plan, as I have said, the ultimate aim of which was to move forward the borders of Serbia to the west.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you claiming that Serbia had aspirations to capture territories such as Dubrovnik and so on over there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what grounds?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: On the grounds of everything that happened. Because the Yugoslav army, especially after the war in Slovenia, acted fully in cooperation with the Serbian leadership, in fact under the direct leadership of you and Boro Jovanovic -- no, Jovic. His surname is Jovic but that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But where did you get this idea that Serbia and I personally could have given orders to the Yugoslav People's Army? There was a conflict between your paramilitary formations and the JNA and not between Serbia and Croatia. Are you aware of that? You were the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: On your behalf, the work was done by the Yugoslav People's Army, which was fictitiously used as a pretext to protect the Serbs, or even a more neutral wording, the separation of the parties to the conflict, but actually always upheld the positions of the rebellious Serbs in Croatia. It armed them, gave them the command personnel, and whenever there were difficulties or dangers of war, it would stand up to the Croatian forces and prevent them from restoring the situation as it was before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kriste. You said it had even more neutral explanations. And this neutral explanation, as you call it, was it not correct that the army was trying to separate the parties to the conflict, the warring parties, and at the same time to preserve and save its own Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. units? Because Kadijevic talks about the pulling out of units from that territory. If somebody wants to occupy a territory, he doesn't plan how to pull them out but, rather, how to deploy them in that territory.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Kadijevic says that once Croatia is completely broken, then he would pull out his units, but not from the whole of Croatia. That is what can be inferred from the context. He would withdraw it from the part of Croatia that would be west of the mentioned line, which would have been the western border of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You really have no factual evidence to corroborate this, but I will not dwell on Kadijevic's book. You can believe me that I haven't read it. I just heard what you quoted, and you misquoted from it. Tell me, please, to save time, you say that for political reasons you were not allowed to get a doctorate, a Ph.D. Who were the political reasons?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with the war in 1990. Actually, I was a member of the Croatian Spring, if that is what you're interested in. And after that, I was persecuted by the police in various other ways for 18 years. Among other things, I was prevented from getting a doctorate, a doctoral degree which was already about to be granted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a representative of the Croatian Spring -- I'm sorry. I'm hearing the French interpretation. I don't know why. Oh, fine. Who persecuted you as a representative of the Croatian Spring; the Croatian police or was it perhaps the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I was persecuted by the Croatian police. Of course within the composition that it was in. But I must say there was no difference there between the Serbs and the Croats. But within the frameworks of the Yugoslav policy that was adopted at the well-known Presidency in that fateful Karadjordjevo in the year 1971 in conformity with that policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Karadjordjevo was the residence of president Tito at that time, and that is where the Central Committee plenary session was held. It could have been held anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, it could have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Karadjordjevo hasn't any importance in that context. There was the Brioni Island Congress as well, and we don't consider them to be fateful or any geographic point, for that matter. Now, do you agree, as you say that you were a participant in the Croatian Spring movement, it was a mass movement, that it was in fact an anti-Yugoslav nationalist movement in Croatia at the time and that to all intents and purposes its objective was for Croatia to secede from Yugoslavia? And actually, what happened later on in continuity, a full 20 years later. Is that right or isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No, it's not. That's not right. The Croatian mass movement, or the Croatian Spring movement, had quite different goals which, unfortunately, proved to be an illusion. The two basic goals that the Croatian Spring movement had are the following: First, the realisation of socialism, as we used to call it, with a human face. That's how we referred to it. And secondly, to turn Yugoslavia into an equitable part of all the republics and ethnic groups within it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that Croatia was not on a footing of equality with all the other republics in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, less equal than Serbia, although Serbia, especially after the death of President Tito, kept saying that it was in jeopardy most in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it divided into three parts under tutorship of some sort all the time? Was Croatia divided? Was Macedonia? Was Slovenia divided? Was any other republic divided except Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Serbia had, with its history, with its historical background, it had two separate provinces, and it was logical to ensure a certain amount of autonomy for those provinces. It had the province of Vojvodina and the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that according to the new constitution of Serbia for which you say rescinded autonomy of these, that pursuant to that constitution it says that two autonomous provinces exist, the autonomous province of Vojvodina and the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija. Before, it just said Kosovo, now it's referred to as Kosovo and Metohija. And because it was Kosovo and Metohija from the very beginning, that was the original name of the province. Somebody found fault with that, I assume, in the course of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, let's try and deal, if we can, with something to do with the witness's evidence. You can, of course, ask him about the time that he was Minister of Defence, and we allow you some latitude, but I think we're getting some way from the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. You're quite right. I do wish to be rational and to use my time rationally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kriste, you cooperated very well with Tudjman from the 1960s, from the latter years of the 1960s, revolving around the Matica Hrvatska. You attended meetings of the Matica, for example, in Metkovic in 1971 when a rally was held when a monument to Radic was unveiled. You were the principal guests there, you yourself and Tudjman; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, that's not the point either. It was a sort of regular activity, political activity of yours. You knew Tudjman very well. You cooperated with him very well. You became the first Defence Minister in the government formed by him after his advent to power in 1990, et cetera. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, you spoke about how Tudjman in 1989 already, way back in 1989 -- so nothing was happening in Yugoslavia then, there were no upsets, no disruptions, especially not Serbo-Croatian tensions. That already in 1989, he had planned the borders of Croatia along the Drina River. That is to say, within the borders that Croatia existed as a quisling creation during World War II, that is to say incorporating Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. So it is within these fascist borders of the fascist NDH, Independent State of Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I didn't say nor did I write that Tudjman had planned the borders of Croatia along the Drina River. All I said was that, in a conversation we had and when discussing -- we discussed the issue and that at that time Mr. Tudjman considered that the Muslims were Croats and that in view of this fact and in view of the historical circumstances, it would be logical for that border to be drawn in that way. However, Mr. Tudjman, operationally or in any other political sense, ever undertook anything in order to put that idea of his into practice. It was a sort of historical, philosophical thinking on the subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you were doing was in fact a philosophical, historical thinking on your part; right? And the upshot of the historical political thinking was that you disarmed the Serbs, you dismissed them from their jobs, and they had recollections of World War II, what happened to them; and of the Independent State of Croatia, they did not have any historical political thought, but they were criminals, looters, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kriste, I have here your own interview. I assume you recognise it. Here it is. It is in your magazine the Nacional. It is printed in Zagreb. I can't see the exact date of this particular issue but we'll find it easily. This is the title page. I'm sure you recognise the interview and know about it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The title of the interview -- first of all, you have your photograph here and then your book entitled "Shadows Over Freedom," and then a quotation by you. Here it is. It says: "Tudjman already in 1989 planned the borders along the Drina River." That's what you claim, and that appeared in the title of this magazine. Now you're claiming differently. Now, I'm going to read this because this is a quotation and in fact your answer to questions put to you by a journalist from your own Zagreb paper, and this is what you say. You say the following: "Somewhat earlier on, the HDZ sent a proclamation to the Croatian people in which I didn't like the portion --" so you were critical towards this proclamation. I'm not quoting you in a negative light here. You say, critically: "I was bothered by a portion speaking about Croatia in its historical and natural boundaries, borders. It was quite clear to me at the very start that it was -- implied borders along the River Drina which had existed only during the time of the Independent State of Croatia. I asked Tudjman that very morning --" and then you have a colon and inverted commas -- "Do you think that the eastern borders of Croatia should be along the Drina River? His answer to me was briefly --" once again under quotations -- "Yes." "I warned him that this was impossible, because in BiH - that is to say Bosnia-Herzegovina - there are only 17 to 18 per cent of Croats living there. His answer was that all the Muslims were Croats, in fact, which was sufficient reason for the entire neighbouring state to be annexed to Croatia. I was surprised because I knew Tudjman very well, and I knew his impassioned idea and affiliation to the Banovina of Croatia." The interpreters have asked me to read a little more slowly, so I shall do so. I will read the last sentence: "I was surprised because I knew Tudjman very well and his impassioned idea and affiliation to the idea of the Banovina of Croatia." Therefore, what kind of Serb militancy, Mr. Kriste, are you talking about when already way back in 1989 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with this in a logical way. First of all about the quotation, Mr. Kriste. Do you remember roughly when that was printed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you. The interview was conducted about two or three months ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says the 3rd of December, 2002 is the date. The 3rd of December, 2002. That is the date on every page of this magazine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, then, since a lengthy excerpt has been played to you -- or read to you, rather, if you want to comment on that, you can. Then the accused can ask you some questions about it. First of all, does it represent what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything you want to say about it before you're asked any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say is this: It wasn't an official body or official meeting of any kind. It was a conversation in which I put forward somewhat different views and assessments than those of Mr. Tudjman, and so our opinions diverged there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. What is it you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was precisely asking him this: Because these aspirations are quite clear - and we'll get to the other point later on, the other area and its functions according to yourself - what kind of Serb militism are you talking about when you bear in mind the fact that it was precisely this new Croatian power and authority that had the aspirations of reconstructing the former NDH, the Independent State of Croatia, and to annex Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I think this has been completely erroneously interpreted to the effect that the new authorities aspired to reconstruct the NDH. This was only a discussion about one particular element related to a border issue. The second point that I wish to stress is that it was not the new Croatian authorities at that time, because the League of Communists of Croatia was still in power at the time in Croatia, and the new Croatian authorities did not take any practical steps along the lines of implementing this kind of idea, nor did it ever become part of the programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, Mr. Kriste, and we're going to digress here a little way: You said that the new Croatian authorities never had any aggressive actions towards -- or ideas towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you know, are you aware that the first instance of violence, the first shooting that took place, the first killings of civilians, unfortunately Serbs, which took place were perpetrated by the Croatian National Guard Corps who had crossed from Croatian territory onto the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina into the territory quite specifically of the Bosanski Brod municipality and slaughtered the entire civilian population in the village of Sijekovac, and up until that time there was complete peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, complete peace reigned there. So do you know about the presence of those formations, of those Croatian National Guard units, the way in which they stormed Bosnia-Herzegovina territory and killed in their masses or, rather, perpetrated the whole -- the liquidation of an entire Serbian village in the Bosanski Brod municipality where there had been no conflicts or clashes or national tensions up until then and nothing that had been going on before that. That was the first armed conflict on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was caused by your own army, the Croatian National Guard Corps, on the territory of a neighbouring republic. Are you aware of that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I'm hearing of that here and now. That that actually happened -- that had that actually happened, I would probably have known of that beforehand. That is why I consider that to be untrue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. There are a lot of documents about that, a lot of documents, and a lot of witnesses to testify to it. I haven't got them all here with me, although I did present them during one of the testimonies here. I think it was the 108th Brigade of the Croatian National Guard Corps, and even some of their certificates and confirmations when they opened brothels and arrested Serb women who were going home during the day and so on. Now, tell me, it is true - because you were a close associate of President Tudjman yourself - that he relied on right-hand political parties which based their entire political programmes on the past, on history?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Right-wing parties. Ah. I wanted to clarify what is meant by right-wing political parties, what I imply, what I mean by them, because Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in our areas where we live, right-hand or left-wing and right wing has not been precisely defined. So I mentioned that in part that they relied on forces, that is to say those forces which were more based on the past, rather than having a clear-cut vision of a modern, democratic Croatia. And that was just one segment of the factors, just some of the factors which represented the real life of the people and trends at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But, Mr. Kriste, in this interview, the one that I've been quoting from, you say that one of his mistakes was the following: That he made a number major mistakes. And then I go in to quote you in this interview, and you say: "First and foremost, it was his reliance on right-wing political parties, political forces, whose political programmes and platforms were based on the past." Those are your words. That's what you said. I assume that you're not challenging that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That is a free interpretation. I didn't dictate the interview. The formulation that I used and that I consider to be correct is what I explained and said a moment ago, that they were forces which were turned towards the past rather than being forward-looking and having a clear vision of a modern, democratic Croatia. And they were not exclusively the forces that were there, that found themselves there, they were just a segment of the overall forces that existed on the Croatian political arena.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also criticised him --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, it would have been better had that not happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah. You say it would have been better had that not happened. Well, then I assume that none of this would have happened had that not happened.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Ah, no, Mr. Milosevic. Had there had not been your policies and your politics --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's the thesis being put forward here by the opposite side, and it's going to fall through, but tell me this: Is it true that he tried to divide up, to carve up Bosnia and that was something that you criticised him for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. We did have information, pieces of information that were never official, and they said that you and Mr. Tudjman had had talks about the structuring of Serbo-Croatian relations in order to find a middle way to satisfy each of your interests on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I was not present, I did not attend your talks, the talks you two had, nor was I there when an official piece of information was published which I myself could see, which would be accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kriste, if you had had access to it, then all that Tudjman could have said to you was that my position had always been that I see the future between Serbs and Croats as relations of friendship and not as relations of conflict and that it was the key relationship in the Balkans, and he knew very well that I had even rejected offers for any kind of alliance to be formed between the Muslims and the Serbs against the Croats, explaining to them the same point; that we do not want to wish to be enemies with the Croats but quite the opposite, friends in the historical and every other sense and in the future. But let me go back. You say here the next major error was the war with the Muslims, the Bosniaks, and the attempt to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that what you reproached President Tudjman for or was this something that you remembered in December 2002 or when you believe that he advocated these policies as a friend of his and a long-standing associate and a person who I believe had the courage to tell him what he thought, did you tell him then that you thought that these were mistakes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I never discussed these matters with President Tudjman directly, but if such policies were to be pursued, I thought they would be erroneous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that those policies were pursued and that they were wrong. Very well. Tell me, is it true that Tudjman, like Susak - and you mentioned that a moment ago - he thought at least that Herzegovina should be annexed to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That is also something I never discussed with Mr. Tudjman, but the information that this was discussed I obtained in an informal conversation with Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allow me to quote you from this interview. Nacional asks you: "Gojko Susak convinced you that the leadership of the HDZ had decided to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina." Your answer, and I'm quoting it verbatim: "Correct. Sometime in March 1991 at the Assembly steps, I met Mr. Gojko Susak. He was in a good mood, and I asked him for the reason, and he answered, 'I'm coming from the old man, or the leader, and we've just agreed that at least Herzegovina should be joined to Croatia.'" That is what you said a moment ago, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me now, what has that got to do with the meeting between me and Tudjman in Karadjordjevo? You say they went to that meeting of theirs and they agreed to join Herzegovina to Croatia. How could you have linked that meeting with this story when they have nothing in common?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: You know best what you discussed. I wasn't present during those discussions in Karadjordjevo. But after that talk, there were rumours to the effect that the substance of those talks related to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you may be -- if you're interested, the talks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may be a convenient time. Mr. Milosevic, just bear this in mind: That you are asking questions, not giving evidence at the moment. There have been some fairly lengthy statements from you. Yes. We will adjourn now, 20 minutes. You can have, after the adjournment, another hour, if you want it, with this witness for cross-examination. We'll then sit until 2.00 in order to try and finish the witness today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid one hour is too little, Mr. May, and I would kindly ask you to consider the possibility of giving me a little more for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will -- it depends how we get on, what use you make of that time. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll want about one or two minutes in private session before the end of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To continue with what we were discussing a moment ago, can we conclude that Tudjman and Susak had agreed to at least join Herzegovina to Croatia, so, by force, to take alien territory. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: They most probably did discuss Herzegovina, judging by what Mr. Susak told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. But the relationship of the new authorities in Croatia towards Muslims is best reflected in the example that you mentioned when Susak said that from Prozor their units would start against the Muslims and that there would be no prisoners of war there. So let me remind you, quoting from this interview of yours, you speak of him and you say: "I knew that he was au courant, and I said, 'Gojko, can anything be done to ease the tensions between Muslims and Croats?' And he answered coldly: 'Of course. A strong unit of ours is heading from Prozor and it will take no prisoners of war.' I was appalled because I realised that Susak was conveying to me the official decision as to what the future Croatian policy would be towards Muslims and Bosniaks." Is that right, sir, Mr. Kriste?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. More or less so. Actually, I did not authenticate that interview. It was a conversation with a journalist but the wording was compiled by the journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the substance is there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to Dubrovnik, the offensive led by Bobetko was no offensive to deblock Dubrovnik but was an attempt to divide Bosnia and capture Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Bobetko, on the sudden battlefield, went there when, according to the Vance Plan, JNA was supposed to leave that part of Croatia. Therefore, it was really to monitor the pull-out rather than a real war operation to liberate that part of Croatia. At least, that was my understanding of those facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you say quite explicitly in this interview of yours -- and let me quote verbatim: "By opening the southern theatre of war with strong forces under Bobetko, this was obviously an attempt to take part in the conquest of Herzegovina and partly -- and a part of Bosnia and only partially Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Nobody could have had the aim of conquering Dubrovnik. The only aim could have been to liberate Dubrovnik. So, yes, my estimate was that those forces were there in a sense to carry out -- in the event of certain developments that could have taken place in the area of Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. Yes, in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. The events on the Dubrovnik theatre should be viewed in the context of those activities of the Croatian army; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: This was happening in 1992. The main operations of the Yugoslav People's Army were carried out in 1991. The open attack on Dubrovnik started on the 1st of September, and the occupation of that area by the Yugoslav People's Army and Territorial Defence forces, volunteers or reservists, however they like to call themselves, from Montenegro and the Serbian part of Bosnia and Herzegovina were -- had been there for all of eight months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but as you are talking about a period when the SFRY still existed as a state and was the only subject of international law, the JNA had every right to be all over the territory of that country, including Croatia, and that was its constitutional duty.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Its constitutional duty was not to wage war against individual republics or nations in Yugoslavia. Its constitutional obligation was quite different; to defend the external borders from a possible external aggressor. And in Dubrovnik, it didn't come there to walk around the Dubrovnik area, it was waging war in Dubrovnik to capture certain territories and place it -- place them under their control against the will of the citizens of Croatia and Yugoslavia. Furthermore, in the spring of 1992, Croatia was internationally recognised and admitted to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you're talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: You're talking about 1992, because Bobetko was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But in the context of these aspirations towards Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. Is there any dispute that the JNA had the duty of defending the territorial integrity and constitutional order of SFRY and to prevent a civil war breaking out in the territory of SFRY? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: What civil war? No one from Croatia was attacking any one. Not a single soldier, or rather, not a single person with a rifle in his hand did not cross the Serbian or the Montenegrin border. The war was being waged in the territory of Croatia. And in view of the rebellious Serbs and with the assistance of the JNA, there were certain Serbia paramilitary units there; the Seselj's men, Arkan's member, Dragan - I don't know what his name was - the White Eagles, and I don't know what. All of them were waging war in collaboration with the Yugoslav People's Army against the Croatian people on Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this brigade of the National Guards Corps that crossed into Bosnia and Herzegovina and committed a massacre in Sijekovac, that was not an armed formation of Croatia that did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has dealt with that. He says he knows nothing about it. It's your allegation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that JNA units on the theatre of war in Dubrovnik had the duty to keep under control their installations, their warehouses, their bases that they had there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The JNA didn't have any facilities of its own in Dubrovnik. No warehouses, no bases. It didn't have anything. It just had a rest home, a vacation centre in Kupari where, I think, you spent your holidays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. For many years, in fact. Tell me, please, do you know -- since I have a video recording of that but because of the briefness of time I can use it with the next witness, perhaps, showing fire being opened from Dubrovnik at the warehouse in Zarkovcia being blown up, which was blown up. Wasn't that a JNA warehouse? And was it not blown up with fire from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I don't know of that particular case, but in Zarkovica, before the 1st of October, 1991, there was no weapons depot of the JNA. It could have got there only after that date. So after the Yugoslav army had entered the territory of Croatia in wartime formation and brought with it weapons and ammunition with which to fire on Dubrovnik. So if that happened, it could have happened only much later, after the 1st of October, after the first attack on Dubrovnik, when the Yugoslav army took control of Bosanka and Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that JNA units in the area consisted of members of at least four Yugoslav republics?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not a personnel officer in the JNA. I just know that in Croatia, the Yugoslav People's Army was being abandoned especially after the conflict in Slovenia. It was being left by members of all ethnicities, including Serbs from Serbia. Mothers came to take their sons home. We provided them protection and created conditions for them to return to their homes, and they simply left the JNA of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the JNA in those days had control of the area near Slano, Mostar, Capljina and Stolac and that not one of these towns was destroyed or damaged while the JNA was there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I know what was happening in the area of Dubrovnik. I couldn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. claim anything regarding Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, this area that you have mentioned, and the Yugoslav army went further from Slano, it reached almost as far as Neum, and wherever it went to, everything was more or less destroyed. You mentioned Slano. There was hardly a single house or hotel that was left intact. Everything was destroyed and razed to the ground and this was done by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you absolutely sure that it was the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Absolutely, because I visited on the 4th of October. Slano was intact and it was then that the JNA entered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that dozens of years before these events, that there were facilities for the defence from the sea and that this whole area had its headquarters in Trebinje, but Dubrovnik and its immediate environs had no military facilities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely what I said. There were no military installations in Dubrovnik and environs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, this area could have been described as a completely demilitarised area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you militarise it then, by organising yourself internally and provoking the army, opening fire at the army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: There was no provocations from our area against the army, nor was fire opened against it. That is completely untrue. We, quite naturally, had a very, very small unit there of the National Guards Corps before the attack, and unfortunately, after the attack too those forces remained of the same size, and we had the police. I repeat, neither of these did ever provoke or attack the JNA. The opposite is true. The JNA attacked citizens, and only then, if they could and to the extent they could, they stood up in defence of the territory and the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the decision of the General Staff? I quoted its number here and -- which states explicitly not to capture Dubrovnik, nor should it be shelled from land, sea, or air?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I don't know if any such decision exists. I don't know of it, but I do know the fact, and the fact is that units of the Yugoslav People's Army attacked and shelled both the town and the whole area of Dubrovnik municipality from the land, from the air, and from the sea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Dubrovnik at that time was in a blockade, according to explanations that have been provided? And we saw something on these screens here, the television footage that was shown with the aim of showing that the barracks were blocked throughout, JNA barracks throughout Croatia were blocked, that soldiers were killed, that it was impossible for the soldiers to be pulled out, to be evacuated from those areas, and so on and so forth. Is that something you know about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I know that no kind of possible evacuation of the Yugoslav People's Army from Croatian territory was ever prevented. Quite the contrary. On several occasions, the Croatian side even lent its men to ensure that the technical goods that the Yugoslav army had there could be taken out of the area when the Yugoslav army decided to do so. And even if it were correct that a garrison was blocked in someplace, are you -- are we responsible for blocking a town in which there were 55.000 inhabitants along with it, all the civilians, and then to target them mercilessly to the end?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about that because Serbia has nothing to do with that whole Dubrovnik affair. So I can't answer that question of yours. However, tell me this, please: As you yourself stated here, that at the end of 1990 weapons were procured, that is to say before the clashes and conflicts began - and during the examination-in-chief, that's what you yourself said - were those weapons procured illegally and unlawfully?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Croatia needed weapons to strengthen its defence within reasonable limits, that is to say to the extent to which it considered that it was under threat and needed to defend itself. Before that, it had been completely disarmed by the Yugoslav People's Army. Let me also mention in this regard that in municipalities where the Serbs were the majority population, the Yugoslav People's Army did not withdraw the weapons of the Territorial Defence but left it. And those were the weapons used in the rebellions. So that's how it was. And also let me mention that Croatia had to step up its police force in those very unstable times when it was quite obvious that the unrest was spreading from the east towards the west and that sooner or later it would reach Croatia, which in fact happened -- was happening in a sense already through the rebellion itself. And so it asked the federal authorities, the military and police authorities, to supply it with a certain quantity of weapons for those units. The federal authorities refused to do that, just like they refused to return the Territorial Defence weapons it had seized which nota bene had been purchased by the Republic of Croatia. So there was no other way out but to procure weapons in the way in which -- it was in the only possible way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kriste. I'm going to quote just one more sentence form this interview of yours, in which you state the following: "The stories that Bobetko liberated the south of Croatia is not true. All he did was accompany their withdrawal with greater or smaller military activity. Therefore, the JNA had withdrawn from the region."

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, it had withdrawn from the region but only in the month of October 1992, which means a full year after having held that territory under its occupation on the basis of the Vance Plan this followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the JNA respected the Vance plan, did it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, but it withdrew one year later, having held that area under occupation in completely inhumane living conditions, and left it destroyed, looted, and burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that is war. That is the war that should never have been waged. And then you say here, when asked, you were part of the so-called leadership: "Did you have any information as to the liquidation of the civilians in Pakrac, Poljana, Gospic and elsewhere when Croatia violated war law?" Your answer was: "No. Let me repeat that the national unity government never discussed Gospic and Pakrac, Poljana and any operations in which war crimes were perpetrated. That something was going on was something reached us through private channels on the basis of contacts. However, I did not know that it was of the scale of which we are seeing it shown today." Isn't that right? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes. It's true that at that time we had no information about those events. Later on, of course, the media put out information of this kind from the first, second, or third areas. Of course it will be up to the Trial Chamber to ascertain the truth, but I consider that any crime committed, regardless of the side committing the crime, should be sanctioned and punished. I should also like to say that it is true that on the Croatian side we didn't just have saints and angels. But, Mr. Milosevic, what your people did in -- on the territory of Croatia is something that only demons could have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're not talking about individual crimes here, and of course we can agree that there were crimes committed on all sides. That is without doubt the fact. But I'm sure you know that in Croatia there was not only unlawful, illegal arming, and you spoke about arming in 1990, but that there were paramilitary formations and units as well.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No, there weren't any paramilitaries in Croatia. Within the frameworks of the police force, the Croatian National Guard Corps was established, which was a legal military formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you comment the following, then, just briefly, please: The decision that was published in the Narodne Novine, issue 32 of the 6th of August, 1990, the rules and regulations as to how to keep records for the members of volunteer youth units of Civil Defence, signed by you as the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a photocopy of the decision, if you'd like to see a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Those are the rules and regulations. But this does not relate to the formation of any paramilitary units. As we can see from the document, they are volunteer youth units who were supposed to work within the frameworks of the Civil Defence or civilian protection system, to come into effect when there were fires. And I must say that there were more fires that broke out in Croatia than there had ever been since 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you not consider this proof of the formation of paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: These were not -- the Civil Defence units were completely legal organisations within the frameworks of the constitutional and legal system that was in force at the time. And these units were just a part of that system, and they were there to help with elemental disasters, as I said a moment ago, for which the Civil Defence units were set up in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as we have pinpointed the goals that you spoke about yourself and the presence of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go on, do you want those regulations exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can exhibit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And while we're on the subject, do you want the interview which you quoted from exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you the interview too. Here it is, the entire magazine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be allowed to make a comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Yes, Mr. Kriste.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian public knows that I am critical towards some aspects of policies pursued by President Tudjman. This is quite evident from this interview too. However, what I consider to be errors in that policy were reflected first of all -- had an adverse effect on our defence preparations, first and foremost, and our subsequent development with respect to privatisation and the development of the economy. However, in no case was it the cause of the outbreak of the conflict on the territory of Yugoslavia. Croatia was attacked. Croatia defended itself, and not a single Croatian soldier crossed the borders into Serbia or Montenegro. And the fact remains that not only the Yugoslav People's Army but the paramilitary units from Serbia and Montenegro did penetrate deep into Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go on, we're going to have numbers for those two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the magazine dated December 3, 2002 will be Defence Exhibit 77, and the decision will be Defence Exhibit 78.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the JNA was a regular, legal, and lawful armed force for the entire SFRY, let's leave it aside for the time being. Are you claiming that a Serb soldier of any kind stormed into Croatia and that some kind of Serb units encroached Croatian territory? And what kind of units, Serb units, would these be that crossed over into Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, different allegedly volunteer units, for example, which were led by Seselj, Arkan, men of that kind. And these units were called the White Eagles, Beli Orlovi, or different names, led by, for example, Captain Dragan, a case in point, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you consider volunteer units to be regular forces of the Republic of Serbia, do you? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Serbia did not prevent their activities, their incursion and crossing of the Serbian and Croatian border. On the contrary, those units cooperated, collaborated, worked together with the units of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in view of what we have just taken note of, the goals and objectives of the forces that you said were highly numerous under Bobetko, up towards Herzegovina and Central Bosnia and so on, this whole situation then on the Dubrovnik and Herzegovina theatre of war, can it only be viewed from the aspects of those broader operations that were carried out or can they be viewed as - how shall I put this? - isolated cases which merit special treatment, taken out of context, out of the context of everything that was going on at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't follow your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was going on in the Dubrovnik and Herzegovina theatre of war, is that only part of the overall idea of taking over occupying Herzegovina and the breakthrough to Central Bosnia by these numerous forces? You said they were numerous forces and that Bobetko was in command of them.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I don't know what the tasks exactly were of those forces, of those troops. What I was saying was based on my free interpretations in the article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, could you give us your own free interpretation of the following: I have here a letter given by the service of the Federal Secretariat for Information. It says that it was authorised to publish a letter of the Federal Secretary, General Veljko Kadijevic, addressed to Lord Carrington, and I'm just going to read several quotations. "JNA units are not attacking the old town of Dubrovnik. They have explicit orders which they are adhering to to the letter not to open fire on the town." I've been asked to read slower. Yes, I'll do so. Second: "The effects of the JNA units in the Dubrovnik region were triggered off by actions and provocation on the part of the armed formations of the Republic of Croatia." And third: "One of its strongholds from which they opened fire at the JNA units, the armed formations of the Republic of Croatia, were located in Kupari, which is a place five kilometres away from Dubrovnik in which there are several military facilities that had previously been taken over and taken control of by the armed formations of the Republic of Croatia, to deblock the military facilities in Dubrovnik on the 25th of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this month have put a cessation to further operations in the region." Is all that correct, what Kadijevic is writing to Carrington?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: What you have just read out is not correct because the Yugoslav Army was active from the 1st of October, and I repeat this for the umpteenth time, and on several occasions shelled the town of Dubrovnik and the old town centre, the old part of the town without any provocation whatsoever on the part of our own defenders. Apart from that, from Kupari, I don't know how anybody could attack the JNA from the town of Kupari unless it was already on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, in its war operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they were army facilities in the first place for peacetime use which had previously been taken control of.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: They were holiday homes, and it was quite natural that when the army launched its attack on Dubrovnik, that our forces then used all the facilities and resources it had at its disposal, including these holiday homes in Kupari. Now, to what extent, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have the date of the letter so it is maybe easier for the witness to answer what allegations are put in the letter and whether they're correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What's the date of the letter, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quoted the date. It was the 26th of October. And in the letter itself, it says: "Today, on the 26th of this month, I sent a proposal to the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, to affect the demilitarisation of Dubrovnik under the control of the European Community." That's what he wrote. And then he adds: "At the time of writing this, I have been informed that the armed formations of the Republic of Croatia in Vukovar opened fire, opened mortar fire on the barracks of that town for the umpteenth time." Then he goes on to speak about the wounding of people there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this information all correct, the information that the federal Defence Secretary General Kadijevic sets out in his letter to Lord Carrington or was he misleading Lord Carrington and the entire Yugoslav public and the Croatian public and all of them together?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Quite obviously he was misleading all of them, because on the 26th of October, it was 26 days after the attack launched by the JNA on Dubrovnik and acted quite contrary to these assertions. It attacked all civilian facilities and destroyed all the installations necessary for the normal life of the community, the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that the aims regarding those operations, judging by what I have in this information, because I only have subsequent information, Serbia has nothing to do with Dubrovnik or that operation? I'm asking you is it true that the targets were only those facilities from which fire was opened against the JNA and which thus became military targets? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That is not right. First of all, JNA units opened fire before any kind of firing on the part of our forces. I told you that earlier on. Even before the 1st of October in Konavle, Brgat, and Komolac. And then on the 1st of October, the JNA and its units also opened fire without any kind of conflict or any kind of resistance on the part of the Croatian side. And it fired on all buildings. It shelled the city centre, even hotels in which refugees were accommodated from Konavle and other parts of Croatia who had previously, especially from Eastern Croatia and Eastern Slavonia, had come to Dubrovnik; but military targets, there weren't any. Only much later when the Yugoslav army had got so close to the town there may have been a few points, but they were always in the open space, outside civilian buildings, and above all, outside the city centre itself. Therefore, those allegations are not truthful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then how do you explain that on the 15th of October, according to what I have here, the JNA entered Cavtat, and in Cavtat nobody fired at the JNA, there was no fighting, and Cavtat did not suffer the least damage. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That is true. Cavtat did not suffer any damage. But all the villages around Cavtat - Zvekovica, Cilipi, Bocici - were destroyed completely. And as I already said, Cavtat entered -- was -- the army entered Cavtat on the basis of a trick. They claimed that they wouldn't go any further than the airport at Cilipi, and as soon as our negotiating team withdrew and went to Cavtat and from there to Dubrovnik, the Yugoslav army entered Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please: This conflict between the army and your paramilitary formations is something that is completely outside the political context of what was happening in Yugoslavia in those days. You were a politician. You were a Minister. Is there a single official statement or decision or procedure on the part of any organ of authority of the SFRY, the Republic of Montenegro, which is a neighbouring republic, or ruling political structures in SFRY or Montenegro who denied the notorious fact that Dubrovnik belonged to the Republic of Croatia and that there were no territorial pretensions towards it or any other part of Croatia? Is there any single statement on the part of anyone from the level of the federal state of Montenegro or Serbia reflecting any kind of aspirations towards any territories outside Serbia or Montenegro, or in this specific case, I'm asking you about Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: It would not be logical for such aspirations to be publicised, but they did realistically exist, and military units followed in implementing those aspirations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, is it true that on the 21st of January, 1991, so many months before all of this, that as part of this militarisation, which was completely unnecessary in Dubrovnik, that the first quantity of ammunition arrived which had been procured for the needs of your units in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No weapons arrived at Dubrovnik airport. That's quite for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 24th of January, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: At least, I have no information about that. But if it had arrived, that quantity of ammunition and weapons would have been in Dubrovnik when the attack started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the staff of Dubrovnik municipality formed on the 6th of September, 1991? What date did you say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The 6th of September. There was a Territorial Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that a whole pattern, plan, project existed for planting mines around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That project could have been designed later when it became quite obvious that an attack on Dubrovnik was forthcoming, when we had firm proof of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true -- what kind of firm proof did you have when that powerful army which was around you didn't capture the city? And it could have if it had wanted to.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: It tried to. On the 6th of December was the last attempt to capture the city. And since that attempt was unsuccessful and as it provoked very sharp reaction on the part of the international community, such attempts to capture the city itself were not continued. But I must say that the whole area of Dubrovnik was captured by the Yugoslav army. The only part that remained free and unoccupied was the city town -- the town itself from Sustjepan to the Belvedere Hotel. This could amount to 10 kilometres or so. Everything else was controlled by the army and occupied for a whole year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the reason for this the formation, in this world renowned tourist centre, the formation of armed units which were a threat to the peaceful life of the population?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Those formations did not represent a threat to the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was their purpose when no one had intention -- no one intended to capture the town?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: And who is telling you that no one had such intentions? The facts point to the opposite. Attempt was made to capture it, and most it was in fact captured. One could assume that that would happen with a great degree of probability, just as it was possible to assume that the war against Croatia would be launched, and it did start very early on in 1991, and that it would be waged in order to move forward the borders of Serbia towards the west.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know of the constitutional declaration of SFRY on the 27th of April, 1992, that it had no aspirations, that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had no aspirations towards any republics after Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina had been recognised?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- I beg your pardon. I am not aware of that declaration, but it is a fact that in those days, about 30 per cent of Croatian territory was under the control of paramilitary units, Serb rebels, and the Yugoslav army.
