utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean the part of the territory in which the Serbs were the majority.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I already said that the Serbs were not the majority in that area. There were more Croats there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the whole of Croatia too. The line to which the United Nations Protected Areas were formed that were out of reach of the Croatian authorities covered almost half of Croatia if you take into account the space between those UNPAs because they cut up Croatia into several parts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, who determined the borders of those United Nations Protected Areas? Was it the UN?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The United Nations simply accepted the existing state of affairs. They kept the borders up to which the Serbs, the rebel Serbs, with the help of the army and these military -- and these paramilitary units had reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they formed the UN Protected Areas to confirm the distribution of the Serb population which was in jeopardy in Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No. This was not in accordance with the territory inhabited by Serbs as the majority population. I've already said that. The Serbs in Croatia, though there were inappropriate statements and acts on an individual basis, they were not in danger. I can state that with certainty. Croatia's policy was not to endanger anyone, and therefore, not the Serbs in Croatia either. That there was a state of rebellion was the result of the very active activities of secret services and agents like Seselj and others who came mostly from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kriste. So you're claiming that there was no militarisation of Dubrovnik before the event that happened precisely in order to provoke and expel the JNA from Croatia. Let us see just a very brief clip of a videotape, please. Just a very short clip, please. I hope the technical booth is ready for it. It's very brief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's not ready --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not ready for the minute, but I think it can be made ready soon. Yes, let's go on a bit, Mr. Milosevic, and we can come back to it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 19th of September, 1991, there was additional arming of Dubrovnik which had already been armed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Dubrovnik was not armed earlier or later. Dubrovnik managed to get hold of some 300 pieces of infantry weapons up until the 1st of October when the invasion occurred. On the 19th of September, there was no arming -- no arms arrived in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that we had here evidence by certain witnesses from your own Dubrovnik who were indicating the positions of mortars, anti-aircraft guns and so on that was moving around and opening fire from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: This could have happened only after the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that on the 29th of September, an order was issued for movement towards the line of separation, towards the border of Montenegro, some 700 metres long, and that as you know, at the beginning of October there was a commemorative service for soldiers who had been killed on the territory of Montenegro by fire opened on them from the territory of Croatia? Do you remember that? There was an Assembly meeting. The leadership of Montenegro held a session in that connection. It was on television.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The killing of Yugoslav soldiers or Montenegrins killed by Croatia did not occur then or later. It could have been published in your newspapers. Anything could have been published in your newspapers. But it is quite certain that there were no military activities along that border on our part. Those activities started quite a bit earlier on, that is, towards the end of September, and they started from the Montenegrin side. I still have friends in the Bay of Kotor. I go there every summer. And what you're now saying no one ever mentioned to me over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't there, I have this information which has been confirmed from many sides. Tell me, is it true that on the 30th of the September that military - I don't know how to put it - line, combat line, was established, 700 metres long, stretching from Brgat to the St. Barbara hill and that, from those positions, fire was opened jointly by members of the Croatian guards, the police, armed civilians, and so on? They were organised into platoons. Is that right or not? Just tell me no if you think that it's not true so that we can move on.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I don't know the exact deployment our forces, but on the 29th of September, that was the day prior to the attack by the Yugoslav army on Dubrovnik. That attack, as I said, was expected, and we had reliable information from a man who came from the Trebinje garrison, and we knew exactly how things were developing. And since that village, Brgat, is on the road, on the Trebinje to Dubrovnik road, and this was the direction from which an attack could be expected, I do not exclude the possibility that certain of our forces were deployed to that village. But in view of the total forces available on our side, the number you mentioned was unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since neither you nor I appear to be familiar with this, and I have here a note, that is the order of the -- precise order of the JNA General Staff, 11-71 of the 4th of the October, 1991, the 4th of October, 1991, in which it says: "Dubrovnik is not to be conquered, nor should Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. artillery or air force fire be opened on it." So you're not familiar with that order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that order, but I am familiar with the fact, because I was present in Dubrovnik on the 1st of October. Four days prior to that order being issued, I know that the Yugoslav army in the territory of Dubrovnik carried out an attack on Dubrovnik from the land, from the sea, and from the air. In that context, I am not interested that four years later the General Staff or I don't know who -- four days later, sorry, may have issued such an order, because Dubrovnik was attacked on a continuing basis from the 1st of September on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to interrupt you to tell you that the tape is now ready if you want it. If you want us to hear it, we need to know what it is. Where does the tape come from? What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The tape was filmed in Dubrovnik itself by their people, and it shows the oath being taken by these men. You will see and you will be able to assess its value yourself. It is very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You got it, then, from the Prosecution, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't get it -- I got it from my associates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You mean the Croatian side. It was filmed by them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs were not present there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This, this is the oath: I swear by all that is holy that I will abide by the Ustasha principles and be guided by the regulations and carry out all orders by the poglavnik or the leader, and I will keep all secrets. I will fight in the Ustasha ranks for the Independent State of Croatia and do everything the leader orders. I swear that I will defend the independence of Croatia within Ustasha ranks. If I violate this oath, I am aware of the consequences and the punishment of death awaits me. May God help me."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be your comment of this? Because it doesn't quite appear to be in accordance with the positions that you expressed in this interview and generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, you can only ask the questions which are fair. All you've shown us is a picture of some not very military-looking people taking some sort of oath in a public house or a cafe. Now, you can ask the witness to comment on it, of course, but you'll have to point out some way you say it's relevant to his evidence and how it contradicts it, because I must say it's not clear to me. Perhaps the witness, having -- the thing having been played, can make some comment on it if there's any.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot make any comments. This is a clip I have never seen. It's obviously a group of young people. Now, where it was filmed -- it could have been filmed anywhere. In any event, this was not a part of Croatian policy, nor was it an official act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not a part of Croatian policy. This was an Ustasha oath, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: This could have been filmed even in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, very well. Fine. I need no further comment. If this was filmed in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I didn't say it was. I said it could have been taken anywhere. And as for Ustasha slogans in Croatia, individuals made them who were secretly in contact with the Yugoslav UDBA and the counter-intelligence service with KOS, and those ideas were intended to compromise the idea of Croatian independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I see. This is a montage of the secret service outside Croatia.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I am not claiming anything definitely. I'm just saying that I do not see that this could have -- by anything that this could have been in Dubrovnik, nor that it could have been organised by any official body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. So you're not aware of the order of the 4th of October, prohibiting any fire being opened on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to stop you because you've put that a number of times and the witness has said he doesn't know about it. Now, your time is almost up. Are you asking for more time with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. I am asking for more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, how long is it you want?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll tell you in just a moment. I have - let me see - about 40 more questions which I have made a note of here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, have you any questions of this witness or can you perhaps get on without it this time, try and finish the witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that there are a lot of things here that could be of use to the Trial Chamber. I don't know what else Mr. Milosevic plans to ask, but as we stand now, I will need some time for my questions, but I'd like to see what Mr. Slobodan Milosevic is going to ask next. I think that there are some very important matters that are important with respect to Dubrovnik and the entire testimony, points that have not been clarified for you to be able to gain full insight into the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quarter of an hour more, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a quarter of an hour more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, also I would like to mention that I need about five minutes because I think there is one error here that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I'm afraid Mr. Kriste is going to have to come back tomorrow to conclude his evidence. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that already on the 8th of October, that is to say four days after this order, that lack of discipline on the part of JNA members was sanctioned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I don't know about that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that on the 17th of October there was intensive action on the part of the Dubrovnik forces using mortars against the JNA positions in the surrounding areas? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. And I don't believe that it is a valid piece of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know in what hotels the Croatian National Guard Corps members and the MUP members were put up? The Tirenja President [phoen], the Revelin Tower, where ammunition was stored, did you have information about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: As to the hotels you just mentioned, there were mostly refugees accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the JNA commanders, via radio Herceg-Novi - and the reception of that radio station is very good in Dubrovnik - that they launched an appeal precisely to the people in Dubrovnik not to open fire on the members of the JNA and that unless they abide by that rule -- and that if they do not do so, there will not be a single shot fired from the other side. This was a call for surrender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was I clear when I said that via radio Herceg-Novi they asked that nobody should shoot at the army and that not a single bullet would be fired by it if nobody attacked the army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, nobody fired until the army began firing at the defenders. The Croatian side just responded when there was firing from the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the JNA members targeted not only from around the town of Dubrovnik but from the old town itself, using artillery pieces? You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Not only do I not know about that but it never happened. There was never a truck with weapons in the old part of Dubrovnik, the old town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that fire was opened from the positions, for example, by the Neptun Hotel where there were the Croatian National Guard Corps and Medarevo, which is where the artillery weapons were from, Lapadska Glavica and that area where there were artillery weapons, and Gorica too. Gradac, the Ploce beach, artillery pieces there too, the Belvedere and Libertas hotels, which is where persons who were armed and uniformed were located, members of the Croatian paramilitary forces. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: From some of those positions, the position that you mentioned, there might have been some military action but only much later on when the Yugoslav army and the attending units closed off -- closed the encirclement, the siege of Dubrovnik. From the Ploce beach side, there was certainly no shooting. And of the hotels that you mentioned, one of our units was only in the Belvedere Hotel because it was our last stronghold or -- rather, it was our last defence point on the eastern side of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 14th of September, at Debeli Brijeg, Vitaljina was the village, that the Zengas or Croatian National Guard Corps had set up mines all over the place and that 200 ZNG members were located in the village of Prsecina at Debeli Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, the Croatian defence never had that many members and, therefore, was not able to deploy them at all these points, whereas Debeli Brijeg is on the Croatian side. It is this side of the Croatian border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it is both on the Montenegrin and Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: They were not on the Montenegrin side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm talking about the frontier. Do you know that on the 23rd of September, for example - this is another point - that members of the Croatian National Guard corps in Vitaljina set up mortars and guns, cannons, and launched provocations on the JNA firing from that side precisely on Montenegrin territory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That piece of information is incorrect. Otherwise, I would know about it if it were correct. At that time, Vitaljina, due to an attack from the eastern flanks, the population had left this area and were put up at the hotels in Babin Kuk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what happened on the 24th of the September in the Ivanica region. On the 24th of September.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Only the 24th of September in the region of Ivanica, the only thing that could happened is this: There could have just been shooting at Brgat, because I arrived on the 26th myself, I got to Dubrovnik on the 26th of September, and upon my arrival, I was informed that from the Ivanica area Brgat and Komolac were fired at, were targeted. The next day, I visited these two places and saw that the information was indeed correct, because several buildings were damaged, some of them were completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is Ivanica on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Ivanica razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: When? When do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Ivanica razed to the ground? Did the Serbs raze it to the ground?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: At Ivanica in 1991, there was quite certainly no Croatian operations. Not a single roof tile was damaged, let alone house. Not a single house was razed to the ground until the end of 1991. I don't know what happened later on when the JNA started its withdrawal or, rather, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say you were in Dubrovnik before the JNA launched an attack on the area. Now, where did the attack come from?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The attack came from two directions; from Montenegro at Konavle, and the main attack on the town itself was launched from this line, the Ivanica line and further along the road towards Dubrovnik and the border which, unfortunately at that particular location is so close to town that you can target the place from the border itself, and it was from Komolac that the town was targeted and, as I said, the infrastructure was destroyed, all the facilities providing the town with electricity and water were destroyed, and planes on that same day knocked down the relay stations on Srdj Hill and transmissions, so those lines were down too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the destruction of these pipelines, is that something the JNA did or did the local forces effect that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: It was probably the JNA with Vucurevic's volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say "probably the JNA"? Do you know whether this was done by the JNA or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: The JNA launched the attack. Now, who was working with the JNA in the attack, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the leadership of the Croatian National Guard Corps, with Spegelj at its head, and the leadership of Croatia sent, on the 30th of July, 1991, a message saying that the JNA should be removed from Croatia, that this was the official policy and an official plan, to remove the JNA from Croatia? In 1991, July.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: That was July 1991. At that time, yes, Spegelj did put forward a plan for Croatia's defence. The details of that plan I'm not familiar with myself, but I wish to remind you that it was one month after the JNA had attacked Slovenia and been vanquished in Slovenia. So it was after this that it looked towards Croatia with even greater force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, that with this attack on Slovenia, even the Slovenian leadership itself, in my presence, said that it had nothing to do with Serbia? We didn't even know about it. Are you aware of that? Is that something you know about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the Slovenian leadership could have told you. All I know is that the Yugoslav People's Army attacked Slovenia and that there was a war on for several days, after which the Yugoslav Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. People's Army withdrew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It attacked soldiers that had no ammunition, did it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that the dynamics of Spegelj's plan envisaged attacks on warehouses and barracks of the JNA, airports, taking over all army facilities within the space of four days? Do you recall that plan? Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, should, after Slovenia, the JNA launch an attack on Croatia, it would be quite logical for a plan to have been devised on the basis of which the Croatian side would come by the means and resources it needed for its defence. But let me also mention that Spegelj's plan was not adopted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was what was done, even if the plan was not adopted.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: No. That was not what was done at the time. Some barracks or, rather, some military warehouses were taken control of later on through the will of the local units - of the Crisis Staff, that is - and that was the only way in which to procure the resources necessary for Croatia to be able to defend itself and stand up to a far superior adversary, which was at the time the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was an agreement reached in Igalo in which it stated that it was of imperative importance that the forces on the theatre of war be separated in order to guarantee a complete and secure safe -- cease-fire and that paramilitaries be disbanded and irregular units and to demobilise the irregular forces of the Croatian National Guard Corps and that the JNA should withdraw to the barracks? Was that what happened or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: I know that there were several agreements. I'm not quite sure now about the contents of the Igalo agreement, but I also know for a fact that the Yugoslav People's Army, for the most part, did not respect those agreements, the agreement reached. What it did was in the areas where armed groups of Serb rebels existed, it would incite their activities and would then take the middle ground and stand up to the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kriste, I have shown you footage of a talk between Tudjman and Kadijevic in which Kadijevic insists upon the fact that Croatia should adhere to the letter of the agreement signed with Carrington and that attacks on barracks be ceased, and he highlighted the attack in -- at the Sibenik barracks, which was under way at the time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Mr. Tudjman believed Mr. Kadijevic when he said that Croatia would not be attacked, and he did indeed take all necessary steps to prevent any kind of action on the Croatian side which could be seen to be some sort of preparation for war. Therefore, in the first half of 1991, Croatia did not import any weapons, and all domestic manufacture of weapons was put a stop to. But despite all this, Croatia was nonetheless attacked and was covered in blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time the then Secretary of National Defence, General Kadijevic, wrote out a written request for demilitarisation of Dubrovnik under the control of the European Community, that the JNA units should be removed from the area and that a life -- normal conditions should be brought back to the town, and this was not accepted by the Croatian side. Do you happen to know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslav army had nothing to do there because there were no military facilities in Dubrovnik. And this talk about the demilitarisation of Dubrovnik, if it came from Mr. Kadijevic, is ludicrous, because to demilitarise Dubrovnik is something that only the Yugoslav army could do because the Yugoslav army had militarised it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is now finished but you can ask another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's very difficult for me now to select one final question from all the ones I have here, but let me take a look. I have quite a number of questions left, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you this in connection with the allegations in General Bobetko's book: That it was precisely in Dubrovnik, in the space of 20 days, that you destroyed 18 enemy tanks without any losses of men on your side. And that is on page 124 of his book. And then on page 125, he says that he selected tactics which comprised of the fact that he should attack the weakest flank of the enemy, which was the infantry, and that they did this night and day, and then you go on to say that he did not throw out the JNA but just witnessed the JNA's withdrawal, as you yourself say in your interview, the interview from which I quoted. So where is the truth there? What is the truth in all of this, Mr. Kriste?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE
utterances.text: Well, I can't say. I haven't got the text. I haven't got the excerpt from Mr. Bobetko's book, and it would be very difficult for me to comment and to say on what particular page of his book he wrote what. But what I can say is how many tanks were actually destroyed and how successful his operation was in the southern reaches of Croatia, all I can say is that all this happened in the second half or, rather, from May 1992 onwards. And in the most difficult part of the war for Dubrovnik and for Croatia in general in 1991, there was no question of us having been able to destroy such large forces on the Yugoslav side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must bring this -- we must bring this to a close. Mr. Tapuskovic, now, have you some questions you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours and Your Honour Judge May, it is very difficult for me to complete this in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have two minutes in closed session after the witness has withdrawn? Nothing to do with him.
